articles.title: Gia công cho nước ngoài, doanh nghiệp có lúc chỉ lãi 1 USD mỗi sản phẩm
articles.text:
Đây là thông điệp được các chuyên gia, đại biểu trong và ngoài nước chia sẻ tại phiên thảo luận Định vị lại Việt Nam và ASEAN trong chuỗi giá trị toàn cầu, diễn ra sáng 27/10. Chương trình thuộc khuôn khổ Diễn đàn Kinh tế Mùa thu năm 2026 tại TPHCM.
Nghịch lý dòng vốn ngoại và "vùng trũng" thương mại nội khối
Theo dữ liệu tại diễn đàn, ASEAN có quy mô kinh tế khoảng 4.300 tỷ USD, dân số 700 triệu người, thu hút xấp xỉ 245 tỷ USD vốn FDI vào năm 2025 (tăng 10% so với năm trước). Tuy nhiên, mức độ gắn kết thương mại giữa các nền kinh tế thành viên vẫn còn hạn chế.
Dữ liệu từ Tổ chức Hợp tác và Phát triển Kinh tế - OECD cho thấy, tỷ trọng giá trị gia tăng nước ngoài trong xuất khẩu của Việt Nam đã tăng từ 33% năm 2010 lên gần 50% vào năm 2022, phản ánh mức độ phụ thuộc đáng kể vào đầu vào nhập khẩu trong quá trình sản xuất hàng xuất khẩu.
Sự phụ thuộc này càng mong manh hơn khi nhìn vào dòng chảy thương mại nội bộ. Ông Sacha Dray, chuyên gia kinh tế thuộc Đơn vị Chính sách Kinh tế Việt Nam của Ngân hàng Thế giới (World Bank) tại Việt Nam, cho biết thương mại nội khối chỉ chiếm khoảng 22% tổng kim ngạch xuất khẩu hàng hóa của ASEAN, thấp hơn đáng kể so với tỷ lệ khoảng 60% của Liên minh châu Âu (EU).
Nguyên nhân xuất phát từ sự lệch pha cung - cầu do khoảng cách thu nhập giữa nước giàu nhất và nghèo nhất khối khá cao, tạo ra sự lệch pha về nhu cầu tiêu dùng. Bên cạnh đó, dù tham gia sâu vào các lĩnh vực như ô tô tại Thái Lan, lắp ráp tại Việt Nam hay bán dẫn tại Malaysia và Singapore, chuỗi giá trị nội khối mới chỉ chiếm khoảng 1/3 mức độ tham gia chuỗi giá trị toàn cầu.
Dẫn chứng từ ngành chế biến gỗ Việt Nam - lĩnh vực xuất khẩu tới 168 thị trường, ông Ngô Sỹ Hoài, Phó Chủ tịch kiêm Tổng Thư ký Hiệp hội Gỗ và Lâm sản Việt Nam (VIFOREST), cho rằng các nhà sản xuất đang đối mặt với các biện pháp phòng vệ thương mại của Mỹ.
Ông cảnh báo mô hình gia công OEM thuần túy theo đơn đặt hàng nước ngoài đang làm triệt tiêu tính đổi mới sáng tạo, khiến các doanh nghiệp trong khối cạnh tranh hạ giá khốc liệt. Khi mẫu mã bị sao chép tràn lan, cuộc đua hạ giá thành để tranh giành đơn hàng khiến biên lợi nhuận ròng có thời điểm chỉ còn 1 USD trên mỗi sản phẩm, thậm chí thấp hơn.
Trước thực trạng này, chuyên gia World Bank đề xuất chính phủ các nước cần thúc đẩy đầu tư nội khối "ASEAN sang ASEAN", tận dụng sức lan tỏa của FDI và sớm hài hòa hóa các tiêu chuẩn kỹ thuật để tạo điều kiện công nhận lẫn nhau giữa các nước thành viên.
Doanh nghiệp cần nâng cao năng lực
Nhìn nhận về giá trị thực chất của dòng vốn FDI, bà Jessica Nguyễn, Tổng Giám đốc ABB Việt Nam, khẳng định: "Nhà xưởng hay máy móc có thể mua sắm và di dời rất nhanh, nhưng năng lực sản xuất và quản trị thì cần nhiều năm tích lũy".
Do đó, thước đo giá trị của dòng vốn ngoại nằm ở việc chuyển giao năng lực lõi qua 3 khía cạnh gồm bí quyết quản trị chất lượng toàn cầu cho người lao động; năng lực giải quyết các bài toán kỹ thuật phức tạp cho kỹ sư bản địa; và việc xác lập niềm tin xuyên suốt chuỗi cung ứng với hơn 1.000 SME Việt Nam dựa trên sự ổn định, an toàn và khả năng truy xuất nguồn gốc.
Ngoài ra, việc sớm chuyển giao tri thức thực tiễn vào giảng đường đại học chính là chìa khóa để chuẩn bị lực lượng lao động sẵn sàng cho tương lai.
Lãnh đạo ABB nhấn mạnh, mục tiêu tương lai của khu vực không dừng lại ở "Make in ASEAN" (Sản xuất tại ASEAN), mà phải tiến lên nấc thang "Engineered and Innovated in ASEAN" (Được thiết kế và đổi mới sáng tạo tại ASEAN).
Minh chứng cho bước chuyển này, ông Ngô Sỹ Hoài dẫn trường hợp của AA Corporation, một doanh nghiệp Việt Nam bứt phá từ nhà thầu nội thất trong nước sang làm chủ thiết kế, đấu thầu trọn gói các công trình khách sạn siêu sang quốc tế như Park Hyatt tại Caribbean.
Nhìn từ AA, ông Hoài cho rằng bài học cốt lõi là phải chọn đúng phân khúc thị trường ngách cao cấp, lấy thiết kế độc bản dẫn dắt hoạt động kinh doanh thay vì trông chờ vào những hợp đồng gia công số lượng lớn giá rẻ.
“Các nước ASEAN có thế mạnh tài nguyên rừng, cần chuyển từ cạnh tranh đối đầu sang hợp tác để cùng nâng cấp năng lực cạnh tranh. Chuyển đổi sẽ không bắt đầu nếu không hành động, và hành động sẽ không diễn ra nếu chúng ta không thay đổi tư duy. Phải tự tin vào năng lực và trí tuệ của chính mình trước khi đòi hỏi niềm tin từ thị trường toàn cầu", ông Hoài nói.
Ở góc độ ứng dụng công nghệ, ông Youxian Zhu, sáng lập kiêm CEO Black Lake Technologies, dẫn chứng từ thực tế một ngôi chùa Phật giáo tại Trung Quốc đã sử dụng AI thiết kế các sản phẩm lưu niệm độc bản (như tượng sư tử gỗ), sau đó chuyển dữ liệu sản xuất đến các xưởng tại Việt Nam và Trung Quốc.
Kết quả, thay vì làm hàng gia công đại trà với biên lợi nhuận ròng dưới 1 USD/sản phẩm, nhà máy thu về biên lợi nhuận từ 10-20 USD/sản phẩm dù quy mô đơn hàng tối thiểu giảm xuống còn 100 sản phẩm.
Ví dụ này cho thấy, muốn tạo ra lợi nhuận thì các xưởng sản xuất phải nhanh chóng thích ứng với mô hình sản xuất linh hoạt.
Sản xuất linh hoạt và bệ đỡ chính sách
Để hiện thực hóa những bước chuyển từ vi mô, bài toán thể chế và liên kết khu vực được xác định là bệ đỡ quyết định. Bà Phạm Quỳnh Mai, Phó Vụ trưởng Vụ Phát triển Thị trường nước ngoài và Thương mại Đa biên (Bộ Công Thương), nhận định rào cản thương mại lớn nhất hiện nay không còn là thuế quan mà nằm ở các vấn đề "sau đường biên giới", như quy tắc xuất xứ phức tạp, thủ tục hải quan và tiêu chuẩn kỹ thuật chồng chéo.
Đối với khối doanh nghiệp nhỏ và vừa (SME), lực lượng chiếm hơn 97% nền kinh tế, đại diện Bộ Công Thương đề xuất triển khai Chương trình Phát triển Nhà cung ứng Quốc gia, thành lập Quỹ hỗ trợ nâng cao năng lực cho SME và đổi mới đào tạo nhân lực theo mô hình hợp tác ba bên.
Bà Phạm Quỳnh Mai kiến nghị ASEAN cần sớm phát triển các cụm liên kết công nghiệp xuyên biên giới trong các ngành công nghệ cao then chốt như điện tử, bán dẫn, ô tô và năng lượng sạch. Mô hình này cho phép kết nối các tập đoàn lớn, doanh nghiệp SME, các trường đại học và viện nghiên cứu ở nhiều quốc gia trong cùng một chuỗi giá trị.
Cụm liên kết sẽ tối ưu hóa lợi thế so sánh của từng thành viên: Một nước cung cấp nguyên liệu thô (như Indonesia), một nước chuyên sâu sản xuất linh kiện linh hoạt (như Malaysia), và một nước đảm nhận khâu lắp ráp chế tạo phương tiện (như Thái Lan).
Việc hình thành các cụm công nghiệp xuyên biên giới không chỉ giúp củng cố năng lực cạnh tranh khu vực để tăng năng lực cạnh tranh với các trung tâm sản xuất lớn như Trung Quốc hay Ấn Độ, mà còn tạo cú hích thu hút dòng vốn FDI chất lượng cao gắn liền với chuyển giao công nghệ.
Quan trọng hơn, đây chính là đòn bẩy thực chất nhất để gia tăng mạnh mẽ thương mại nội khối, kéo các vùng phát triển thấp hơn cùng tham gia vào chuỗi cung ứng bền bỉ và hiệu quả của ASEAN.

articles.title: This old Nokia phone got an AI Upgrade it was never designed for - Engadget
articles.text:
This old Nokia phone got an AI Upgrade it was never designed for
The GOAT of dumb phones gets a new lease on life.
Nearly 20 years ago, Nokia released the Nokia 6300. Despite arriving the same month Steve Jobs would introduce the iPhone at MacWorld 2007, the 6300 would go on to become one of Nokia's best-selling phones, thanks to its understated but attractive design, affordable price and easy-to-use software. In 2026, however, the original 6300, not to be confused with the recent 4G rerelease, is a device on borrowed time.
For one, it's a 2G phone, and finding a carrier that still operates its old 2G network is becoming more difficult with each passing year. Then there's the phone's browser, which Nokia never updated to work with any internet security protocols beyond TLS 1.0. After Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla came together to deprecate the standard in 2020, less than an estimated 25 percent of all websites support TSL 1.0 connections as of mid last year, meaning the 6300 essentially can't access the modern internet. There's not much that can be done about the former, but one coder has devised a pretty clever solution to get around the 6300's dated browser using the latest chatbots.
Meet AIKON
In late September, Turkish entrepreneur Emir Karşıyakalı took to X to show off Claude S40, an app he vibe coded to make his old Nokia 6300 a bit more useable in 2026. In its original form, his app app allowed the 6300 to connect with Claude over a Java and Go backend. Since then, Karşıyakalı has updated the software to make it work with all of the major chatbots, including ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok, and renamed the app Aikon — that's Nokia spelt backwards — to reflect the greater compatibility.
Outside of a phone running either Nokia's S40 or S60 operating systems, you'll need a Go server to hold the API key from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI or SpaceXSI. This part of the equation is essential since it's the server that communicates with Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok, and truncates their responses into 8kB blocks your old phone can read. It's also worth mentioning, since you're going through each company's API, you'll need to set up token billing.
For what is ultimately a gimmick, Karşıyakalı's app is quite robust and thoughtful. There's an reading mode, with a dedicated keypad shortcut, to make using a chatbot on the 6300's 240x320 display a bit more manageable. Provided you a memory card, you can also save responses to the 6300 for offline reading. If you want to send photos to your favorite chatbot for analysis, you can do that too. It's even possible to send voice messages up to 30 seconds long, with an OpenAI model handling the speech-to-text conversion. Over on the server side, Aikon will hold messages for up to 30 days, and the app supports English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Russian, Indonesian and Turkish. Karşıyakalı has open sourced the app so others can continue building on the app.
Now, before you dig out your old Nokia phone, just know if you live in the US there's no way you'll get this app running. That's because the nation's last 2G network went offline this summer when T-Mobile shut down its old GSM network in August. If you live outside of North America and want to try Aikon out for yourself, head over to Github and follow the installation instructions.

articles.title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Financial giant Bank of America is reminding customers to bank safely by kindly not sharing your banking credentials with your AI agent.
In an email blast to customers titled “Protecting your finances in the Al World,” Bank of America urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, “including an Al-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf.”
You can practically sense the frustration in the person sending the email. Still, customers are increasingly handing over their log-ins as personal AI assistants grow more popular. Sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account.
This latest warning comes as banks are still exploring how AI agents fit into the financial world but are reportedly grappling with unauthorized agents accessing their customers’ money. As we discussed onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, banks, payment providers, and processors are still trying to figure out how to allow customers access to their bank accounts using AI tools, such as for agentic payments, which allow people to set agents to autonomously buy things at the best price or the right time.
A spokesperson for Bank of America confirmed the authenticity of the bank’s email that was posted to social media. But heed the bank’s warning, for if things go wrong, it’s on you. Account agreements at most banks hold customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to. “If you do share your credentials,” its email reads, “keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access.”
(via Bryan Toporek)

articles.title: Cái kết bất ngờ khi thử nghiệm 15 robot hình người tại nhà máy ô tô: Chậm hơn sức người 2,7 lần nhưng báo hiệu ngày tàn của lao động truyền thống?
articles.text:
Tại Chiết Giang (Trung Quốc) Leju đã đưa dàn robot hình người Leju Kuavo vào thực chiến tại nhà máy sản xuất linh kiện ô tô, những con số báo cáo trả về vừa khiến người ta bật cười, nhưng cũng vừa mở ra một góc nhìn khiến ai cũng phải lạnh gáy.
Tốc độ "rùa bò" và con số "thành công 98%"
Theo số liệu được công bố, dàn robot Leju Kuavo thực hiện các thao tác nhận diện, cầm nắm, vận chuyển và đưa các linh kiện kim loại nhỏ vào trạm sản xuất. Tuy nhiên, các báo cáo ghi nhận tốc độ hoàn thành mỗi chu kỳ của robot kéo dài chưa đầy 40 giây, chậm hơn khoảng 2,7 lần so với thời gian thao tác trung bình 15 giây của một công nhân con người.
Bên cạnh đó, hệ thống ghi nhận tỷ lệ thành công đạt 98%. Con số này tương đương với tỷ lệ lỗi khoảng 2%, tức xuất hiện hàng nghìn trường hợp lỗi trong tổng số 60.000 linh kiện được xử lý. Các chuyên gia vận hành đánh giá rằng tỷ lệ sai sót này là lớn, đòi hỏi phải có sự can thiệp và kiểm soát chặt chẽ để tránh phát sinh chi phí xử lý sự cố.
Theo Leju, đợt triển khai này không chỉ thử nghiệm phần cứng mà còn là môi trường thực tế để huấn luyện các hệ thống AI thể hiện (embodied AI) của Leju. Cụ thể, 15 robot này đã có khả năng tự động điều chỉnh chuyển động để thích ứng với sự thay đổi vị trí của linh kiện mà không cần sự can thiệp thủ công từ con người.
Sự nguy hiểm không nằm ở 40 giây "rùa bò", mà ở 40.000 bản ghi dữ liệu AI mỗi tháng
Dù các robot hiện tại vẫn có khoảng cách về tốc độ thao tác so với con người và cần thời gian hoàn thiện các tiêu chuẩn khắt khe trong sản xuất, việc đưa robot hình người vào chạy thực tế tới 1.000 giờ ngay trên dây chuyền thật cho thấy tốc độ phát triển và thử nghiệm nhanh chóng của ngành công nghiệp tự động hóa tại Trung Quốc.
Dự án mở ra hướng đi mới trong việc tích hợp công nghệ AI vào hạ tầng sản xuất, đồng thời đặt ra bài toán dài hạn về tối ưu hóa hiệu suất và chi phí cho các doanh nghiệp trong kỷ nguyên sản xuất thông minh.
Điều đáng sợ nhất trong bản báo cáo này không nằm ở việc con robot đang làm nhanh hay chậm, mà nằm ở văn hóa thử nghiệm của các nhà máy. Họ dám đưa công nghệ mới tinh vào chạy thực tế ngay trên dây chuyền sản xuất thật, thu về hơn 40.000 bản ghi dữ liệu vận hành mỗi tháng để liên tục huấn luyện mô hình AI.
Con người mất hàng nghìn năm tiến hóa để đạt tới giới hạn sinh học với chu kỳ thao tác 15 giây và không thể ép nhanh hơn nữa. Ngược lại, con robot mất 40 giây ở giai đoạn này chỉ vì nó đang trong quá trình tích lũy dữ liệu thực tế (real-world training).
Với tốc độ tối ưu phần cứng và thuật toán đáng sợ của các kỹ sư Trung Quốc hiện nay, việc kéo thời gian từ 40 giây xuống 20 giây hay 15 giây chỉ là câu chuyện của thời gian. Khi bài toán tốc độ và giá thành được giải quyết triệt để, áp lực cạnh tranh toàn cầu sẽ thay đổi hoàn toàn cục diện.
Tốc độ "rùa bò" hôm nay và hồi chuông báo tử cho lao động truyền thống
Nhìn vào khoảng cách tốc độ khi robot chậm hơn con người tới 2,7 lần, nhiều người dễ lầm tưởng rằng lực lượng lao động chân tay vẫn đang nắm giữ vị thế độc tôn an toàn. Tuy nhiên, kết quả từ 1.000 giờ thực chiến tại nhà máy ô tô không phải là minh chứng cho sự yếu kém của cỗ máy, mà chính là những nhát cuốc đầu tiên đào sâu vào nền móng của mô hình sử dụng lao động truyền thống.
Khi các bản ghi dữ liệu liên tục được thu thập để tối ưu hóa thuật toán, ngày mà robot hoàn thiện tốc độ, sự khéo léo và bài toán chi phí cũng là lúc hàng loạt công nhân chân tay đối mặt với nguy cơ bị thay thế triệt để.
Cuộc thử nghiệm này không chỉ đơn thuần là câu chuyện về 15 cỗ máy, mà là lời cảnh báo rõ ràng rằng kỷ nguyên hoàng kim của sức lao động cơ học đang thực sự đếm ngược từng ngày./

articles.title: UK Politician Jess Asato Got Deepfaked. Now She’s Taking xAI to Court
articles.text:
Few people understand the current deepfake epidemic better than Jess Asato. The British Labour MP has spent years campaigning against the use of technology to abuse women and girls. Then, after calling out Elon Musk during the notorious Grok Deepfake Scandal of 2025, Asato found herself caught in the very crisis she had been trying to prevent.
Disturbing and degrading deepfake images of the MP circulated widely. One appeared to depict a sexual assault. When Asato reported them to X, the platform repeatedly dismissed her complaints. So she decided to take the fight somewhere else: the courts. She is now pursuing legal action against Musk’s xAI, arguing that it unlawfully used her image without her consent. The case could help establish a precedent for holding AI companies accountable when their products cause harm.
For Asato, this is personal, but it is hardly new territory. Before entering Parliament, she spent years working with charities supporting survivors of domestic abuse and vulnerable children. That experience has shaped her political career, informing her push for stronger protections for women and children online. Now, she is confronting more troubling questions: What happens when the technology enabling abuse becomes ubiquitous, the platforms hosting it refuse to intervene, and the people targeted are left to fight back on their own?
At stake for Asato is more than the misuse of a single image. It is whether consent still means anything when AI can manufacture almost anything, and whether the companies building these tools can be made to answer for what they do. Asato is betting that the law can catch up with the technology. And she is prepared to take on Musk to find out. (xAI did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Also, before you read on, be aware that this interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ROSIE SWASH: Jess, I just want to have a couple of warm-up questions before we get into it. Tell us a bit about your background, how did you end up becoming MP for Lowestoft?
JESS ASATO: Sure. So, I grew up in East Anglia in Norfolk and Suffolk, and in a not very political family. I got the politics bug in 1997 when Tony Blair was talking about education, education, education. Having experienced it, I felt that we could be doing a lot better in our education system. So I joined the Labour Party and got involved with my local groups.
Before Parliament, I worked for the largest children's charity in the UK for three years on their policy and public affairs, trying to change legislation on behalf of the most vulnerable children in the country. Six years prior to that I worked for a domestic abuse charity called SafeLives where we did huge amounts of work to try and improve the situation for survivors of domestic abuse, particularly through the Domestic Abuse Act.
Those twin issues of women and children have become my focus in Parliament, and I’ve been very clear that my reason for being here, my mission really, is to be a voice for women and children.
Well, that’s a good entry point for us to start talking about this year. So in early 2026, there was widespread reporting on Grok, xAI’s chatbot, being used to create sexualized images of children and women, and those images being circulated on X. How aware were you at this point of the phenomenon of deepfakes being used in this way?
Very aware, and actually had been working with survivors who had experienced deepfakes for quite a number of years. Ever since the advent of AI this has been happening to women, and there’s also been developing risks of children both being put into child sexual abuse material and also children using nudification tools on other children, thereby criminalizing themselves because these tools are so easy to access and often free.
So I was already very alive to the huge harms being created by AI deepfakes of both women and children before Grok ever happened. It was a known harm, which is why many of the tools from other companies had already taken steps to stop them from being used to create this kind of content.
There are a number of tools where, if you type in “nudify,” or “take the clothes off this person,” the tool will refuse to do that. So into that environment came Grok.
Was there a particularly egregious example or incident prior to Grok when you became aware of deepfakes that really stuck with you?
There is a brilliant campaigner who goes by the name of Jodie. I think it was probably listening to the experiences of Jodie, who was deepfaked, and it was such an affront to her that somebody would do this, and then she found out it was actually a friend. Such a betrayal of trust.
These things destroy not just the individual involved, but often families and everyone around them too.
For people who don’t know, who exactly was Jodie? Is this a constituent of yours or someone who came forward to you specifically?
No, no, no. She's a very well-known campaigner on this issue. That’s not her real name.
I know it sounds obvious, but what exactly is nudification?
It is where you ask an AI tool to take the image or video of a real person and use generative AI to make that person either nude, partially nude, or engaging in pornographic acts. This is something that, because of the photorealistic nature of AI images, it has become increasingly hard to see what is a fake image.
It can often look incredibly, incredibly real.
So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal earlier this year that made you want to raise this in the House of Commons?
It was the fact that we already knew that you could stop this from happening by designing the AI tool to reject the ability to do this.
This was completely avoidable. That’s why I spoke out, but also because I’d just spent a year and a half campaigning to get a ban on nudification apps, and here was an all-purpose AI tool becoming a nudification app.
It just felt to me as though we were making strides in the UK, and then the world’s richest man and his product decided to turn the clock back.
So what exactly did you stand up and say?
What I did was I talked about the need for the government to accelerate its ban on nudification apps, which it did. So the then secretary of state for science, innovation and technology, Liz Kendall, said that she was going to bring that ban into law through the Crime and Policing Act, which she did.
But I also said that it was very important that we went further than that, because, of course, Grok itself is not a sole-purpose nudification tool. It has a general use, and therefore we needed to bring all AI chatbots under the auspices of the Online Safety Act. That is also what eventually happened in the Crime and Policing Act, and we’re now waiting until that legislation comes into effect. There’s got to be a consultation, I understand, before it does.
So technically another Grok could happen in this period, but in the future there would be much stronger measures that we could take against tools like Grok creating nudification content.
So that’s a really positive outcome of your interjection in Parliament, but what else happened as a result of you standing up?
Well, one of the things that happened was that I posted on social media saying that Elon Musk should stop Grok from being able to do this.
And then, of course, I became a victim of the same trend. So Grok put this woman in a bikini. And most of the images were sort of pornified, I would say. They weren’t nude images, but they were me with inflated boobs in a bikini.
Then people tried to make it funny, I guess, by putting a swastika on me or hammer and sickles. Or making me pregnant with quintuplets and putting me in a kitchen. Because of course that’s the only use for women—birthing and making dinner. But the really disturbing one was a video of me being surrounded by a group of men, chloroformed over my mouth, and then I fall backwards onto a chair. Then my skirts are lifted up. So no nudity, but clearly the next frame is meant to be a sexual assault. So it was really distressing and disturbing.
That was the point at which a friend said, “You probably need to reach out to a lawyer.” Because each of these things we reported to X, and none of them contravened their terms and conditions. We just kept getting those sort of repeat emails coming back. “We’ve looked into this, and there’s nothing to see here.” So I did engage a lawyer, who sent a letter to X to ask for these to be removed, and they were.
But it was at that point that he said, “I think you might actually have a case. We think that xAI have broken the law.”
It’s impressive how you handled it, but it must have been really awful.
It was; it was awful. This is done to demean, to degrade, and to push women out of online spaces. From my perspective, I tend to use bad or difficult things that happen as a way of thinking about how we change this for the future.
My old boss was an amazing woman called Tessa Jowell. She used to say to me, “How do we change this negative energy into something positive?” “How do we work our way out of this into a place where we actually feel that we’ve learnt from it?”
So I guess she instilled in me that sense that when something bad happens you’ve got a choice. You can wallow in it, you can try and forget about it, or you can use it as a catalyst for change.
So I was quite trepidatious about the idea of taking on a legal action. Not least because of the person who is at the top of xAI, now SpaceXAI. [Eds. note: The company recently rebranded itself as SpaceXSI.] He’s the world’s richest man. But also because I didn’t want myself to necessarily be the story. Many, many women had things that were created of them through both Grok and other nudification tools that are much, much worse.
Having said that, I knew that if there was the opportunity to say that actually they’d broken the law, there was an important point of principle on behalf of all of the women and the children whose images were manipulated and misused by Grok, who would never, ever be able to bring a legal case. So I decided that I wanted to do this, because I wanted to be able to show that no one is bigger than the law.
Doesn’t matter how rich you are or how powerful you are or how big a reach you have in terms of your social media presence or who your friends might be at the top of various governments. If you break the law in our country, you need to feel the force of that. As an ex-lawyer and now as a legislator, it is important that we uphold our law where it has been broken.
So it’s also about giving control back, I think, to us as individuals, but also as a society. So many of these digital changes have been done without our consent or say, and I think there’s a feeling that there’s a sort of runaway train that we’re all on, whether we want to be or not, because we all need to use online spaces for our work, for connection.
And so my view is that we should be expecting companies to respect our law or at least make new laws to bring them more into line with what society really needs.
You said that you gave it some thought. In that moment of trying to decide how to respond, what are you weighing up? Who are you talking to? Are you going back and talking to your team or your family to work out how you should respond, knowing that it may invite further speculation and further attention?
My family mostly, my husband in particular. It’s one thing being a politician and arguing your case to change the law on behalf of women and children; it’s another having your own legal case.
So I was worried about the impact that that might have on my family, my children. I also know that this can bring danger to politicians. So I worried about the fact that I am obviously engaging and making the defendant somebody who has got this very wide reach on social media. However, I don’t like bullies. I very strongly believe that it’s important to fight on the field that you’ve got, and this was an opportunity I felt to make a difference.
So I weighed that up and thought that it was worth having that kind of attention and potential danger, because there is a bigger issue here that we need to get right.
When you say you don’t like bullies, are you talking about, let’s face it, men who used Grok in this way in the first place, or are you talking about Elon Musk?
I’m talking about the men who use this as a form of trying to push women out of the online space. Actually it was quite clear in quite a lot of the comments that they were saying, “Well, if you don’t like this, then get off the platform.”
Either that or, “If this is too hot for you, get out the kitchen,” which I always find quite funny because they put me in a kitchen. I think it’s really interesting when you look at X in terms of its demographics in the UK, it’s highly weighted toward men. I think some of that’s down to the fact that there is just so much misogyny and abuse on it. So I’m assuming, and correct me if I’m wrong, that the other side of the response to going public is that other women have come forward to you.
Absolutely. Actually, one of the heartening things has been people coming forward and saying, “Thank you, because this has now given me the license to actually accept that what happened to me wasn’t my fault. It’s not my shame.” So, in a way, what I’m hoping is that this has helped some victims to process what has happened to them and understand that this was not right.
I’ve also had emails from parents where they’ve said that this has happened to their daughter. It’s been done by boys at school. I’ve had teachers saying that boys have made pornographic AI imagery of them. And it’s something where we’ve just sort of let it happen and wash over us and accept that somehow this is now a part of the society we live in.
So yes quite a number of people have come forward. Obviously not all of their experiences have been through Grok, and I think one of the things is that often, when you see these films or images, you don’t know what platform they’ve been created on. I mean, the only reason why I knew it was Grok was because it was integrated with X, and you could see the commands that had been given by the users.
But much of the time, when this content is created, most victims don’t know by whom or on what platform. And so there’s really very little they can do about it. And I think it’s that sort of sense of helplessness that you have been violated, and that is the word that comes up so frequently from victims of this particular issue.
It’s not just that it’s nudified. Of course, much of my content wasn’t. It’s the lack of consent. And lots of people say, “Oh, but it’s fake. It’s just a laugh.” But what people don’t understand is that it is hyperrealistic, and it’s your face.
It’s a piece of your soul. It’s not just pixels on the internet. It is a person. And because obviously I’ve worked for a long time in violence against women and girls and spoken to many victims of sexual assault and to children who’ve been victims of child sexual abuse, it is the lack of consent that is so disturbing.
It can leave people with PTSD and quite deep trauma. And there have been a number of people I’ve met who have said that the world seems less safe to them because this has happened to them.
I think you’ve already touched on it, but what is the biggest myth around deepfakes that you would wish to dispel?
That it comes without any harm.
That it’s just a laugh.
There is clear harm, even when it’s not done to demean or degrade. So even if it’s done sometimes by friends, the fact is that you haven’t consented to that. There is something about the human psyche which is that when you see yourself so realistically created in a different situation or scenario, something that’s not something you would have done, I think it’s quite discombobulating.
I think your brain can’t quite process it because your brain knows it’s not true, but it looks very true. And I think psychologically we still don’t really understand how this content is going to change the way we think about our world, how we know what is true and what isn’t true.
Right.
Now, of course, you can do fantastic things with generative AI. All I’m calling for is that we respect people’s consent, and that’s why one of the things I’ve been working on since this happened is to look at whether we could create a system of consent to be manipulated by AI.
Could we create a greater right over our likeness online so that there’s a new social norm, which is that no, you can’t copy and paste that picture into an AI chatbot and do whatever you want with it. That’s not yours. It’s not your data. It’s their data, and you’re breaching the law if you do that.
I think if we were to do that, we could have a wide range of applications. It wouldn’t just be in this space of the sexualization of women and children. But also with political disinformation. We are so close to a moment where somebody produces a hyperrealistic video of a politician saying something that they didn’t, and then that leads to real-world harm. And so we’ve got to find a new social norm that says unless for public figures it’s parody or satire—and absolutely you’ve got to protect that—but in all other instances your picture, your voice, and your moving image is your personal data, and it’s not for anyone else to use.
So that’s interesting because you’re touching on new social norms and the possibility of new laws to keep up with this technology. But your lawsuit is specifically under a data law. Talk to me about that versus a law around consensual imagery or deepfakes specifically.
So, my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR, the data protection law, and it contends that Grok misused my data without my consent. It didn’t have consent to process my data, the data being my face and my likeness. But also under privacy laws that I had a reasonable expectation of privacy and that particularly the video of me being prepared for sexual assault reaches a criminal threshold and that nobody should be expected to be on the receiving end of.
Let’s remember, this is actually a product that has been designed by software engineers and developers, and that actually products should not lead to an invasion of privacy and the harm that I then experienced as a result of that, including distress and a sense that I was being harassed by this particular creation of this particular video.
So, it rests on good solid legal grounds, and we await the defense from SpaceX AI.
I don’t know how much you can say, legally, but what part of the process are you in? What happens next? What’s the timeline for a resolution to this case?
So like with a lot of legal cases, it’s very, very hard to pin down a timeline. But my understanding is that we should be receiving the response and the defense from SpaceXAI in the near future. But we don’t have a deadline or a particular time that I can put on it.
After that, my understanding is that the case will then be looked at, and if there is a case to answer, then it will go to a court hearing. But once again, no idea when that might be. And I think there’s lots of legal things that I don’t understand that need to be worked out in the meantime as well between my lawyers and their lawyers.
Have you ever had any acknowledgment on X itself from Elon Musk or anyone at xAI about this case? Has he ever spoken publicly about it?
No.
Would you expect him to?
I don’t think so. They clearly want to challenge this case, and so the best place to do that, I think, is in the courts and to leave it to see whether the merits of the case come through.
You were in New York recently to address the city council about your case. You didn’t get to speak to anyone directly at the company, is that right?
No. I mean, despite being subpoenaed, they didn’t turn up. Four of the other frontier AI companies did attend under subpoena. SpaceXAI didn’t, but they eventually did get their hearing with SpaceX in the city council. So, they have now had their opportunity to put questions and indeed did raise my case with them, I understand.
Was it a little enraging to attend a hearing like that where a company that you’re suing doesn't bother turning up?
I think it’s quite rude to the elected members of the New York City Council when you are a business that operates in New York. Indeed, I was told that they were just a few subway stops from City Hall. So I had traveled quite a long way from England to be there. And they couldn’t be bothered to turn up, which yeah, it felt arrogant and a bit of a snub, but they’ve now got there, so that’s a good thing.
Since you made the decision to take this to the courts, there have been a number of proposals in Parliament, notably there was a proposal for a kill switch bill at one point. Now I believe it’s dead or it’s not going very well. Is that right?
So, yes, there have been proposals put forward for a kill switch. And my understanding is the government rejected that. There continues to be strong calls for regulation of particularly superintelligent AI. We’ve heard various theories, whether it’s 2 percent, 10 percent, 20 percent risk of human extinction from this sort of race to superintelligence, a recursive AI, and we wouldn’t allow those margins of risk in any other sphere.
We would not allow it in bridge building or airplane making. They didn’t even allow it when they were testing the nuclear bomb and the Trinity test. It feels to me as though so much of this decision-taking is outside of democratic structures. It’s not with the public. It is being done by some incredibly, exceptionally wealthy companies and organizations who say they have the interests of the planet at heart.
But each time, actually, they’re asked about whether that is the future of humanity or whether they think that these risks could kill humanity, there’s a sort of shrugging of the shoulders and, “We’ll just keep going because we want to make money,” I guess.
It has been reported in the British press that there are members of Parliament, some of whom are working on committees to do with technology, who still don’t really understand what AI is. And clearly you’re not one of them because you’re aware of the dangers of this issue. But do you feel working across parties that you’re still having to explain technology and its dangers and possibilities to people who are making laws, or should be making laws, to protect the public from AI?
Well, look, I don’t think that’s only the case about AI. We are humans after all, and we have to deal with every single subject that exists under the sun. We have to get our heads around things that we’ve never heard of before.
A bit like being a journalist actually.
That’s true. But you have to then make laws and decisions. So, I don’t want to be unfair to my colleagues.
You may be a specialist in housing policy and you then need to get your head around AI. But I would say that this is the most important issue in front of anybody in parliament or politics at the moment, and therefore, everyone needs to get their head around AI.
My background is in social policy for women and children. But because we did quite a lot of work on the Online Safety Act when I was working for a children’s charity, we campaigned to get the age verification ban for children in pornography into the OSA. And indeed, created quite a strong piece of legislation in respect of that.
We had to get our heads around online safety on the online space. The problem was, of course, that act didn’t include AI chatbots. There were a number of amendments that tried to get it in and we would’ve been in a much better place had we actually succeeded.
But you know, I’m still not a tech expert even though I had quite a while to try to understand these things. But my view is that this is definitely the new front line of where harms are occurring. We can see that hugely in the increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material, which is absolutely exploding.
In the end it comes down to the people who create the products. And that’s why we should be seeing digital product regulation in the same way as we would any other product regulation.
I’m very, very hopeful that the government is going to look at it really, really closely because there are always design choices that you can make and that can help to prevent these harms, these harms that are completely knowable. We can predict these harms, and so it should be easy to design them out from the start.
Companies can put in more safeguards. Why don’t they?
Profit. But also, let’s be honest, these are global tools and companies. So unless you have international agreement it is a bit like playing whack-a-mole, isn’t it?
The person who made that horrible video of me being chloroformed lives in the US, so the police aren’t gonna follow it up because they’re out of the country.
Do you know who did it?
I don’t know who they are, but the police did find who they were because it’s a criminal offense what they did. They just weren’t able to bring the charge.
We’ve spoken in the last 40 minutes about the full spectrum of human awfulness. I don’t think there’s any area of it that we haven’t …
Oh, sorry. Welcome to my life.
I’m really struck by how cheerful you are despite this. How do you remain so upbeat and hopeful while dealing with all of this?
Because you’ve always got to have hope for the future. I do have a really strong conviction that with the right group of people pushing toward a goal, you can achieve that. You don’t have to accept that things will always be like this. When people come together, when communities come together, you can act for change.
We’re just about to introduce our ban on strangulation in pornography, which is another thing that I’ve been campaigning for and introduced an amendment last year, which the government accepted.
There are always things that we can do to change. You just need to keep going. And also I would say that when you work with these terribly dark areas, yes, it can be quite vicariously traumatizing. But actually the people who work within the sectors are some of the most hopeful people, partly because if you lose hope, then it’s really bad. And we can’t because we’re talking about protecting vulnerable children, and we are fighting for women and our rights to be free of this harm.
How to Listen

articles.title: Why does the FCC hate Minions routers? - Engadget
articles.text:
Why does the FCC hate Minions routers?
The viral Minions-shaped routers are caught by the same ban as TP-Link.
Seen a Wi-Fi router in the form of a Minion in your feed lately? It isn't AI; it's a real product from the South Korean networking company Davolink. Kevin, the taller of its two Minions routers, went viral after an X post last month called it one of the best Wi-Fi 6E routers money can buy. The post drew millions of impressions and Amazon's stock, priced at $62.99, was gone by the next day.
Unfortunately for Minions fans, the FCC treats the router version of Kevin and Bob like every other overseas consumer router. Since March, the agency has banned all new foreign-made network routers from getting the authorization they need to go on sale in the US, unless the manufacturer has an exemption. ASUS, Eero and Netgear all have exemptions, but Davolink isn't. So, while the two existing Minions routers stay legal to sell, we're not going to be seeing a Wi-Fi 7 Minion stateside anytime soon, and firmware updates for the duo are only guaranteed through the end of 2028.
Kevin vs. regular routers
Davolink first showed the routers at CES back in January 2023, under an exclusive design agreement with Universal and put them on sale in South Korea that summer. Kevin, AKA DVW-632, is a tri-band Wi-Fi 6E router that stands at 9.6 inches tall, with a 2.5 Gbps WAN port, one gigabit LAN port, WPA3 security and mesh support. Its AXE5400 rating breaks down as 573 Mbps on the 2.4 GHz band and 2.4 Gbps each on 5 GHz and 6 GHz. Bob, the DVW-642, is the smaller one, a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router with a gigabit WAN port and a top rating of 1.77 Gbps.
Davolink's core business is supplying gateways and access points to the country's three big carriers, SK Broadband, KT and LG Uplus. The US government's vulnerability database has only one entry for a Davolink product: a weak password flaw in a DVW-3200N router from 2018. It was rated 9.8 out of 10 for severity and fixed with new firmware.
The taller Kevin's AXE5400 rating puts it in the same class as TP-Link's Archer AXE75. RTINGS, which has tested both, says the Minion comes out on top in terms of speed and range. But while the more traditional-looking Archer has four gigabit LAN ports, Kevin has only one, so anything beyond one wired device will need a network switch. Wi-Fi 7, the generation after Kevin's, adds 320 MHz channels and lets a device use several bands at once.
How the FCC ban applies to Davolink
The FCC added "routers produced in a foreign country" to its Covered List on March 23. That addition was triggered by a national security determination it received three days earlier from an interagency body convened by the White House. Equipment that makes it onto the Covered List can't get the FCC authorization a wireless device needs before it can be sold in the States. Law firm Wiley's interpretation is that "produced" covers any major stage of making a router, including design and development, regardless of the nationality of the company.
Routers authorized before the March listing can still be imported, sold and used, and the FCC authorized Kevin and Bob between November 2023 and February 2024. Listing also bars changes to authorized devices, software updates included. The FCC has waived that for things like security patches and compatibility fixes until at least January 1, 2029, which is why banned drones and routers in the US will still get critical updates until 2029, and its engineering office has said it will recommend writing the waiver into the rules. If that doesn't happen, and the date doesn't change, Davolink will have to stop patching Kevin and Bob after 2028.
Exemptions, which the FCC calls Conditional Approvals, are granted by the Department of Defense or the Department of Homeland Security and last for up to 18 months. Applicants must disclose where every component and the firmware come from, justify building abroad and commit to a dated plan for US manufacturing, including spending figures and quarterly progress reports. Netgear was approved on April 14, Eero on April 22 and ASUS on September 9. Davolink, which has reported operating losses since 2022, hasn't publicly said whether it has applied for a Conditional Approval.

articles.title: Bong bóng AI Trung Quốc vỡ, 480 tỷ USD vốn hóa bốc hơi chỉ trong chưa đầy 4 tháng
articles.text:
Ngay cả các cổ phiếu công nghệ bán dẫn, robot, trung tâm dữ liệu của Trung Quốc, dù từng rất được ưa chuộng cũng đang phải chứng kiến cảnh giá giảm một nửa so với mức đỉnh của mình.
Cơn sốt cổ phiếu AI và bán dẫn tại Trung Quốc đang đảo chiều mạnh mẽ. Chỉ trong chưa đầy 4 tháng, chỉ số STAR50 đã giảm 40%, thổi bay khoảng 480 tỷ USD vốn hóa thị trường. Đợt bán tháo không chỉ khiến nhà đầu tư thua lỗ mà còn đặt dấu hỏi về khả năng duy trì đà tăng trưởng của những doanh nghiệp công nghệ từng được kỳ vọng trở thành động lực mới của nền kinh tế Trung Quốc.
STAR50, chỉ số tập trung vào các doanh nghiệp AI và bán dẫn, đã lao dốc sau một đợt tăng nóng kéo dài. Trong khi đó, chỉ số CSI 300, đại diện cho nhóm cổ phiếu vốn hóa lớn của Trung Quốc, giảm khoảng 20% so với mức đỉnh hồi tháng 6.
“Thị trường chứng khoán sau đó đã biến thành một đợt tăng điên cuồng mang tính đầu cơ. Và giờ đây, chúng ta đang chứng kiến bong bóng vỡ”, ông Dong Baozhen, một nhà quản lý quỹ tại Bắc Kinh, nhận định.
Điều đáng chú ý là cú sụt giảm diễn ra sau khoảng hai năm thị trường tăng trưởng nhờ kỳ vọng vào các biện pháp kích thích kinh tế. Bắc Kinh từng muốn xây dựng một thị trường tăng trưởng ổn định hơn, thay vì lặp lại chu kỳ tăng nóng rồi lao dốc. Tuy nhiên, đà tăng quá mạnh của cổ phiếu công nghệ đã khiến mục tiêu này gặp thêm thách thức.
Những cổ phiếu từng tăng hàng trăm phần trăm nay mất một nửa giá trị
Mức độ điều chỉnh thể hiện rõ ở những doanh nghiệp từng được nhà đầu tư săn đón. Cổ phiếu Unitree, nhà sản xuất robot nổi tiếng của Trung Quốc, đã giảm một nửa kể từ khi lên sàn vào tháng 8, dù lượng đăng ký mua cổ phiếu của nhà đầu tư cá nhân khi đó cao gấp 8.000 lần số lượng chào bán.
Trong ngành bán dẫn, CXMT mất hơn một phần tư giá trị chỉ trong một tháng. Hai doanh nghiệp MetaX Integrated Circuits và Moore Threads Technology, từng tăng lần lượt 700% và 400% trong ngày giao dịch đầu tiên năm ngoái, cũng đã mất khoảng một nửa giá trị kể từ tháng 7.
Đà giảm còn lan sang các nhà sản xuất linh kiện quang học phục vụ trung tâm dữ liệu. Cổ phiếu Zhongji Innolight và Eoptolink Technology đã giảm khoảng 60% so với các mức đỉnh hồi tháng 6 và tháng 7, một phần do Washington tiến gần hơn tới việc cấm các doanh nghiệp này cung cấp thiết bị cho trung tâm dữ liệu tại Mỹ.
Đằng sau những con số đó là tâm lý thất vọng của nhiều nhà đầu tư cá nhân. Chen Wensheng, một chủ doanh nghiệp nhỏ tại tỉnh Hải Nam, cho biết ông tham gia đợt tăng giá vì tin rằng chính quyền Trung Quốc ủng hộ các công ty như Unitree, vốn có sự tham gia của những quỹ được nhà nước hậu thuẫn. Hiện ông và bạn bè đang phải gánh chịu các khoản thua lỗ.
Theo Goldman Sachs, cổ phiếu AI chiếm tới 42% tổng vốn hóa thị trường và 57% giá trị giao dịch của nhóm cổ phiếu niêm yết tại Trung Quốc đại lục và Hong Kong. Vì vậy, cú sụt giảm không còn giới hạn trong một nhóm doanh nghiệp công nghệ mà đã ảnh hưởng đến đông đảo nhà đầu tư trên thị trường.
Định giá vẫn cao dù thị trường đã lao dốc
Nguyên nhân của đợt bán tháo không xuất phát từ một sự kiện đơn lẻ. Giới giao dịch đề cập đến mức định giá quá cao, các khoản thuế phải nộp và nguy cơ Mỹ hoặc những quốc gia khác cấm thiết bị Trung Quốc được sử dụng trong trung tâm dữ liệu.
Đáng lo ngại hơn, sau khi giảm mạnh, cổ phiếu trong chỉ số STAR50 vẫn giao dịch ở mức khoảng 100 lần lợi nhuận trong 12 tháng gần nhất. Con số này thấp hơn nhiều so với mức đỉnh gần 250 lần, nhưng vẫn cao hơn đáng kể mức khoảng 30 lần của Nasdaq 100 tại Mỹ.
Khoảng cách định giá khiến nhà đầu tư lo ngại đợt bán tháo chưa kết thúc. Ông Hong Hao, đối tác điều hành kiêm giám đốc đầu tư tại Lotus Asset Management ở Hong Kong, cho rằng diễn biến hiện tại sẽ khiến nhiều doanh nghiệp phải tạm dừng kế hoạch niêm yết.
Niềm tin suy giảm cũng có thể cản trở mục tiêu huy động vốn cho ngành công nghệ. Khi nhà đầu tư chuyển sang các tài sản phòng thủ hoặc chờ mức định giá thấp hơn, những doanh nghiệp cần tiền để mở rộng hoạt động sẽ khó thu hút nguồn vốn trên thị trường chứng khoán.
Dù vậy, không phải mọi nhà đầu tư đều xem đợt điều chỉnh là dấu hiệu cho thấy triển vọng công nghệ Trung Quốc đã kết thúc. Một số quỹ vẫn đánh giá tích cực thị trường này, cho rằng việc giá cổ phiếu giảm có thể tạo ra cơ hội cho những nhà đầu tư lựa chọn cẩn trọng. Tuy nhiên, nhiều người tại Trung Quốc đại lục vẫn chờ định giá hạ sâu hơn trước khi quay lại mua vào.
Một rủi ro khác nằm ở cạnh tranh giá. Ông Wang Zhuo, nhà quản lý quỹ tại Shanghai Zhuozhu Investment Management, cho rằng các nhà sản xuất chip và nhà cung cấp AI Trung Quốc cuối cùng cũng sẽ phải bước vào cuộc chiến giảm giá, giống những ngành sản xuất khác của nước này.

articles.title: Who's really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.
Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.
First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.
Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.
Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.
Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.
Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.
Here’s what all that looks like:
The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.
At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.
The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.
If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

articles.title: Apple iPhone Duo vs Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold: The differences beyond foldable style - Engadget
articles.text:
Apple iPhone Duo vs Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold: The differences beyond foldable style
Everything you need to know before buying a foldable phone from Apple or Google.
The iPhone Duo and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold are two of the most premium foldable smartphones on the market, but they prioritize different things. Apple opts for a "passport-style" design, while Google sticks with a more traditional squarish foldable screen. The specs differ significantly, so you'll want to consider a lot before buying either. From screens to cameras to performance, here's how the iPhone Duo differs from the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.
Size, screens and build
The iPhone Duo's wider, passport-sized design is not exactly a new form factor — Samsung also embraced it with its Fold 8 this year — but it still stands out. When closed, its outer screen is 5.4 inches across. Unfold it, and you get a large 7.6-inch screen, approaching the size of the iPad mini's display. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is different, with an 8-inch inner display and a 6.5-inch outer display.
There's no right or wrong answer, so consider what's best for you. The Duo's wider aspect ratio makes it better equipped for consuming content when it's open, but the external screen may seem small. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is the opposite. The square aspect ratio makes some content — like vertical or widescreen videos — look a bit odd, but the external screen is much closer to what you'd find on a conventional smartphone. Speaking of screens, each one has its own unique features. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has brighter screens, peaking at 3,600 nits. The Duo only reaches 3,000 nits, but its foldable screen has a nano-texture layer to reduce glare and minimize the crease.
The iPhone Duo is also heavier and thicker, weighing almost 9 ounces (254 grams) and measuring 11.3 mm when closed. The Pixel weighs 8.4 ounces (239 grams) — it may not sound like much, but you can feel the difference after holding it for a long time.
It's also thinner than the iPhone, at just 10.1 mm. Even so, Engadget's review of the Pixel 11 Pro Fold notes that it also feels significantly bulkier than Samsung's foldables. Neither is really thin by today's standards. The materials differ, too: Apple uses a titanium frame and Ceramic Shield glass on the back, while Google opted for a fiberglass composite back and its own ceramic glass on the outer screen. Both are IP68-certified for water and dust protection, which is still relatively rare among foldable phones.
Software, cameras, battery and price
Apple has attempted to optimize iOS 27 for the iPhone Duo's form factor, adding unique Duo-only features like split-screen mode. The interface also adapts to any orientation you choose — from closed to open and even in "tent" mode when it's half-folded and propped open on a table.
Despite Google's optimizations and several years' head start, Android still doesn't always take full advantage of foldable phones. Many apps simply stretch their interface to fit the larger screen, rather than displaying additional controls or different actions when you open or close the screen. It'll be interesting to see what proportion of iOS developers adapt their top apps for the iPhone Duo once buyers have it.
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold has a big advantage in the camera department. In addition to a 48-megapixel main camera, it also features an ultra-wide and a telephoto sensor for optical zoom, each with 10 megapixels. Engadget's review called it the best camera system on any foldable, despite its ultra-wide and telephoto sensors having lower resolution than those on the standard Pixel 11 Pro. The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel cameras—wide and ultra-wide— but no optical zoom or variable aperture like the iPhone 18 Pro.
It's still hard to compare battery life, especially since the iPhone Duo hasn't hit stores yet. Apple claims it lasts up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner screen and up to 44 hours on the outer screen. The thing is, real-world usage figures can be quite different. Google's foldable lasted about 27 hours during review testing, playing video on the external screen, more than the 24 hours the company promises. However, on charging, the Duo has the edge, reaching 50 percent in about 20 minutes. That is, of course, with a 60W power adapter. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is limited to 30W max charging and takes 30 minutes to reach 50 percent.
Then there's the price: the iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage, but it can go as high as $3,199 for the 2TB version. The iPhone Duo hits stores on October 23 — though you can already set up your pre-order it on Apple's website. You can already buy a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which starts at a slightly lower price of $1,899 with 256GB of storage. The prices are pretty close, so the decision will come down to your priorities for foldables. Do you want a killer camera, or do you already prefer iOS? That will make your decision easier.

articles.title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
articles.text:
Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.
Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.
“I’m kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.
Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.
“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. “We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.
Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.
Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.
What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.
“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”
At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.
“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.
The two initial Direct feeds are aimed at corporate clients. The first, which launched this fall, gives the AI agents of Axios Pro Deals subscribers access to merger and acquisition content. The second feed will act as a source to train in-house large language models, and will launch next year.
Starting with feeds aimed at businesses makes sense. Corporate budgets tend to have more tolerance than individual subscribers for experiments, especially if these unproven concepts could offer even a slight business advantage. But the third Axios Direct feed, which the company plans to develop next year, will be consumer-facing—a way for individual subscribers to have Axios’ reporting sent directly to their agent. All three feeds will look similar to RSS feeds—not aesthetically pleasing, as they aren’t intended for the human eye, but instead taking the form of standardized lines of text.
While Axios is trimming its (already brief) content to satisfy AI, Every is taking a different approach. The six-year-old tech media and software company, which announced a $2 million funding round from investors including LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman last year, expects its subscribers to treat AI as almost an extension of themselves.
Every’s founder Dan Shipper says the most common way Every’s content differs from a typical article is that its writers include prompts in pieces whenever possible, allowing readers to test concepts themselves. An article about a new model, for example, includes a series of prompts the reader can copy-paste into AI, demonstrating how the model answers questions and evaluates input.
Certain types of articles—such as guides—also include buttons that readers can press to “Read With Claude” or “Read With ChatGPT.” Clicking pulls up a prompt, instructing AI to “Start with a tight summary: one paragraph, bulleted. Then offer to go deeper.” Writers pack stories with details without worrying about losing readers’ attention, knowing agents will pick out the most relevant bits.
Two years ago, the outlet launched its first “extendable” article: a long-form feature accompanied by a database of reporting, from interview recordings to news articles to YouTube videos. Readers could query a chatbot, which would fetch additional details from the database.
Recently, Every published a 8,000-word article about Codex that subscribers can consume in even more forms. Drawing from the database, subscribers’ agents can tailor a new piece—be it an article, podcast, or video—to suit their interests. One reader might want a bulleted summary, while another could request a short film of interview bits.
“As a writer, you have to make choices about what goes into the story you’re telling,” Shipper says. “And there’s always a question about, are those the right choices? Or, are those the right choices for a particular reader?” With AI, journalists no longer choose.
“People are gonna do crazy, crazy stuff with this,” Shipper adds.
As outlets eye AI agents as a new audience, another question looms: Can publishers actually make money off of this?
Rasmus Kleis Nielsen, a professor of communication at the University of Copenhagen, says that while the market of publishing for agents is “emerging,” it remains immature and “extremely uneven.” Major questions remain, he says, about price points and how AI agents will interact with content in the future.
Cameron and Allison Murphy, Axios’ chief operating officer, are optimistic about AI as an audience proxy. According to the executives, Axios’s short-form, highly structured style has already made the publisher a favorite for AI to pull from, when responding to prompts. “Time is money for crawlers,” Murphy says. “They don’t want to have to go three quarters down the page to find the main point. So, that’s something that’s already benefiting us.”
But does AI crawling its content actually benefit Axios’ bottom line? Even if readers don’t actually visit the Axios homepage, the brand visibility in and of itself can be positive, Nielsen says. It’s not unlike publishers making content for social platforms like TikTok and Instagram that rarely bring viewers back to their websites.
Publications in general are grappling with how difficult it has become to monetize certain types of content when a chatbot can offer up answers on a silver platter. People only want to pay for information that other publications—and LLMs—don’t have. At Every, that means in-the-weeds guidance on AI and how to use it; at Axios Pro Deals, it’s speedy access to information that could move the market. An all-access Axios Pro Deals subscription costs $2,499 a year, while an annual Every subscription costs $288.
Shipper sees that $288 as a subscription for a human reader, along with their agents. “I may not want to read all of your stuff every month,” Shipper says. But if his subscription can include his agent, “I may want my agent to know it so that it can tell me, ‘Hey, this thing is important.’”
Murphy says that Axios’ starting point is one of acceptance: People are already using AI to absorb information, and that more people will be doing so in the near future.
“I also try to make it a little less existentially terrifying by thinking, this isn’t the first time this has happened in media,” Murphy says. People get their news via social media, via short-form video, via podcasts. “It isn’t really AI as the audience,” Murphy adds. “It’s AI as a tool that helps us reach our audience.”
