articles.title: Anthropic's political problem will get worse before it gets better - Engadget
articles.text:
Anthropic's political problem will get worse before it gets better
Its IPO paperwork reveal a company rightly worried about its regulatory future.
Anthropic filed paperwork to go public on Monday, and while its list of business risk factors spans the fanciful (sentient AI) and the mundane (losing its executives), one stands above the rest as a likely source of headaches in the near future: the "evolving and uncertain regulatory and political environment." With an expected IPO around mid-November, and new representatives from the midterms elections to be sworn in in January, the company has a scant few months before it's almost guaranteed to incur even more political headaches.
While the current Republican-controlled Congress has not put its political will behind constraining AI companies — either the technology they produce or the resources they consume — Americans of both parties are largely agreed in their opposition to data centers and concern about AI displacing jobs. With the executive branch already willing to create difficulty for Anthropic, the predicted "blue wave" of the midterms may result in the company landing on the wrong side of the legislative branch too.
Anti-data center sentiment has absolutely been a factor in the midterms. As of this August, CNN found both Democratic and Republican candidates had spent more than $35 million on campaign ads opposing data centers, with nearly 8 percent of video ads, up from 1 percent a year earlier mentioning data centers.
NBC News currently ranks Ohio's senate race as a toss up, and the candidates' stance on data centers could be the deciding factor in the election. In a private memo from August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned Senator Jon Husted of Ohio could lose his seat entirely due to his track record on data centers. "More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted's neck," the memo read. "If he loses and datacenters get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one." In 2025, the Ohio Chamber of Commerce found that the state gave $2.5 billion in tax breaks for the facilities from 2017 to 2024, a period during which Husted was lieutenant governor.
Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown meanwhile has made opposing data centers the center of his platform. "They eat up our land. They swallow up our water ... then once they're built, our electricity prices go up," Brown told supporters at a recent rally. He has labelled Husted "the face of data centers," calling him the "reason" there are more than 200 data centers across the state. Recent polling from The New York Times found voters believed by an 11 percentage-point margin that Brown would do a better job than Husted would managing the development of data centers.
In other Senate, House and gubernatorial races, the divide on data centers between Democrats and Republicans hasn't been so clear cut. New Jersey's respective hopefuls, Adam Hamawy and Watson Coleman, have both advocated to slow the expansion of data centers, of which there are at least 80 in the state. In Pennsylvania, Governor Josh Shapiro and his opponent Stacy Garrity have accused each other of flip-flopping on the issue, but broadly Democrats have advocated for policies that would make it more difficult and expensive for companies to build data centers.
In Texas, both Democratic Senate and gubernatorial hopefuls James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa have vowed to work toward repealing a bill Governor Greg Abbott signed in 2015 giving hyperscale data centers 20 years of tax breaks. Talarico's platform also calls legislation that would require new facilities to use closed-loop cooling systems, and give local communities the authority to reject data center developments in their municipality. Recent polling shows Talarico with a narrow lead on his opponent, despite Elon Musk spending more than $276 million to aid Republican Ken Paxton. If Talarico wins, he would become the first Democrat to represent Texas in the Senate since 1993.
Candidates in other battleground states have called for even more stringent regulation of AI companies. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed's "AI Under Control" proposal calls for a pause on AI model training and the creation of a Cabinet-level government agency that would inspect AI labs. Like his cohorts, El-Sayed has also advocated for restrictions on data center buildouts.
Current-term Democrats are already getting their shot against the highly unpopular AI industry and its constituent data centers lined up. Oregon's Ron Wyden has proposed plans to strip tax breaks from these facilities; Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, have backed legislation to pause the development of AI models themselves. With the public broadly behind the issue of reining in this industry and a voter mandate in the form of a blue wave, Anthropic might have smartly timed its IPO to buy a few months reprieve before the political environment becomes more hostile and public sentiment turns even more sharply against AI.

articles.title: Invesco brings its model portfolios into Anthropic's Claude for advisers
articles.text:
Invesco is working with Anthropic to let financial advisers use its model portfolios and practice tools inside Claude for Financial Advisors. CAIS, Conquest and FINNY added their own connectors the same day, a day after Anthropic filed for its IPO.
Invesco is working with Anthropic to bring its model portfolios into Claude, the asset manager said on Tuesday. A new Invesco link, or connector, will let advisers who use its portfolios see that data inside Claude for Financial Advisors.
Anthropic launched its tool for advisers in September, as part of a push into finance that began in May. It hooks Claude up to the portfolio, research and planning tools advisers already use.
The Invesco link also gives advisers its research on how to run and grow their firms. It adds a referral scheme with ready-made scripts. Advisers can use Invesco’s ready-built portfolios or build custom ones with the firm.
Invesco manages $2.5T for clients. Clint Harris runs its solutions and custom strategies unit.
“We are excited to roll out Claude-connectivity, which will allow existing model advisors to have greater access,” he said.
Invesco said the tool is for education only and is not investment advice. It warned that AI answers may be wrong or out of date, and must be checked before anyone relies on them.
Other firms are plugging in too. CAIS, Conquest and FINNY, which make software for advisers, added their own Claude links this week, WealthManagement.com reported. That came a day after Anthropic filed for its IPO.
Anthropic has rivals in the field. London’s MDOTM, whose AI platform is used by Morgan Stanley and Amundi, raised $27M in July.

articles.title: Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls
articles.text:
The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”
The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.
“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”
Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.
“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”
These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.
Officially, the Department of Homeland Security has said that it has no plans to deploy ICE agents to polling locations on Election Day. “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED, but added: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”
For the past six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out possible deployments to voting locations during the midterms, even though they would be illegal under federal law. When asked in May if he would deploy the National Guard or ICE during the midterms, Trump said: “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections.”
“Why are there objections to sending ICE officers to polling places?” Todd Blanche, then acting attorney general, said in July. “Illegals can’t vote.” The White House did not respond to requests for comment.
Some election experts simply don’t believe it will happen: “ICE and troops will not be at the polls,” David Becker, a former Justice Department trial attorney who is now head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said at a recent media briefing. “It won't happen. If it happens at all, it will be isolated. It will be accidental. It just won't happen.”
But for organizations on the ground interacting with voters in communities that have been targeted by ICE during Trump’s second term in office, the reality feels very different. Hundreds of different groups are part of the fight against possible ICE intimidation at the polls, and they are all working in coordination with each other.
“I've been up and down this state, in and out of Reno, in and out of Las Vegas, into our rural counties, and the number one question I get is about federal agents at polling locations,” Cisco Aguilar, the Nevada secretary of state, tells WIRED.
Beatriz Lopez, the executive director of Voto Latino, a group encouraging Hispanic and Latino citizens to register to vote, agrees, particularly when it comes to the communities her organization is focused on.
“We know that Latino voters are in the crosshairs of this administration because we know our electorate, our voting bloc, is what's going to shape and determine the elections of so many competitive races,” Lopez tells WIRED. “There is legitimate fear among our community.”
Lopez’s group, like many others WIRED spoke to, will be operating a war room on Election Day, with the specific goal of identifying and debunking viral disinformation that could dissuade citizens from voting. But they are also preparing for more troubling, real-world concerns.
“One of the scenarios that we're anticipating is that at the same time that we're trying to get people out to vote, there might be home raids by ICE in some of these neighborhoods, which has a real chilling effect on people,” Lopez said.
To combat this scenario, groups like 614 ICE Watch in Columbus are organizing patrols in neighborhoods near polling locations. “We send our folks in pairs or in groups. We never want to send anyone alone; we always want to have multiple people there so they can help take control of the situation,” Baiman says, adding that they have trained volunteers in a unique method of de-escalation: “If it starts to get very tense, we teach our folks to hum, to sing, to calm themselves down.”
The goal is not to interact with ICE agents but to document what they are doing so that events can be properly recorded and shared publicly. In January, just days after Alex Pretti was shot and killed in Minneapolis, more than 200,000 people logged into an “Eyes on Ice” Zoom training session, designed to teach people how to properly document ICE activities. Those skills are now being deployed during the midterm elections, Ezra Levin, cofounder of Indivisible, a group founded to stop the rise of authoritarianism in the US, tells WIRED.
On a much smaller scale, Living United for Change in Arizona has been training volunteers to become “constitutional defenders” in person, as the group prepares for next week’s vote. To track ICE activity, the group created a heat map that volunteers use to log and track ICE activity. The map is not available publicly, but WIRED was given access to the website and reviewed hundreds of recorded incidents of ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties.
Groups are also using social media to draw attention to what is happening. Last week in Sutter County, California, six ICE vehicles showed up in the parking lot of the Yuba City board of elections building, where a ballot drop box is located. Following a call from a local resident, NorCal Resist, a mutual aid organization, was able to send one of its trained volunteers and post an alert on Instagram.
“They don't like the attention, [and] when there's more community attention, they do often leave,” Giselle Garcia, programs director with NorCal Resist, tells WIRED.
DHS denied it was conducting immigration enforcement at a polling location, and said its agents were conducting a targeted enforcement operation against an illegal immigrant from Mexico. “ICE parked in front of a polling center—with permission from a representative of the center—while waiting for the target to exit the courthouse,” Chandler Rebel, a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED.
Much of this work, however, is being done in private, a move Lopez says is necessary to protect the online infrastructure they have put in place over the course of the past two years. Levin said that Indivisible’s leadership team would be hunkered down in an Airbnb in an undisclosed location on Election Day, on alert to deploy their sizable resources wherever they are needed.
Despite the fear that pervades minority communities about what Trump and his federal agents will do next week, every group leader, activist and volunteer WIRED spoke to in recent weeks has repeated one central belief: They are prepared.
“You have all this traditional election protection infrastructure that's really, really robust, but then there is this grassroots infrastructure,” Jill Garvey, executive director of States at the Core, which combats authoritarianism and political extremism, tells WIRED. “They've done all this tactical documentation training. They know how to be constitutional observers, and I'm pretty confident that when and if we have an uptick in federal enforcement at the polls, it's going to get documented really, really quickly, and it's going to be beamed out to the world that it's happening.”

articles.title: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
articles.text:
On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.
Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.
It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints unceremoniously dumped on them at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.
All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.
- The mathematics result appears striking. It purports to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. Roughly speaking, the problem asks how little space is needed to rotate a needle or pencil in every direction. A proof of the three-dimensional version was among the achievements for which NYU mathematician Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year. Brown University mathematics professor Brendan Hassett told The Verge OpenAI’s claim “looks well supported,” though he stressed he had not yet checked the Lean formalization, a means of computationally verifying results.
- The physics result explores the Standard Model, the most successful and complete theoretical framework in physics. It concerns quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong nuclear force, one of nature’s four fundamental forces (alongside gravitational force, electromagnetic force, and weak nuclear force) and its relationship to Yang-Mills theory, a cornerstone of modern particle physics. Yang-Mills theory is also at the heart of one of the seven Millennium Prize problems in mathematics, though OpenAI’s work does not address the unresolved “mass gap.”
- The final result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption in theoretical computer science that certain problems cannot be solved substantially faster than brute-force approaches. It is closely related to P versus NP, another Millennium Prize problem and one of the field’s biggest unsolved problems, which asks whether problems whose solutions can be easily checked are also easy to solve.
Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to The Verge said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”
“It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”
But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.
Most experts The Verge spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.
“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge. “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.
“My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset.”
It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had previously pledged to consult on how to share its findings, warned against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.
Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:
”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades.
We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in our recent statement, understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”
Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.
”Fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution ... the papers are difficult to read and verify.”
Finding a way to communicate with researchers in the fields OpenAI is increasingly encroaching on that satisfies everyone may be impossible. The company says it is experimenting with different approaches and acknowledges that each has tradeoffs. “My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset,” said Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman. “So it’s just a question of finding the least offensive option.”
Xiaoyu He, a mathematics professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology, thinks the problem is deeper than how OpenAI chooses to announce its findings. ”The results are very impressive,” he said, “but I think they are making a show of trying to be responsible and thoughtful about how they release results while not being able to change the main issues: that fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution, and that the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

articles.title: Google’s Genie 4 world model adds audio, more realistic worlds, and real-time steering | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google DeepMind released its newest world model, Genie 4, in research preview on Tuesday. The latest model generates the most photorealistic and interactive worlds yet, allowing users to type prompts mid-simulation to change the scene. The model also generates real-time audio that matches the simulated world, including music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue.
The release of Genie 4 comes a couple of months after AI video startup Runway released its second world model, GWM Worlds 2, a playable model that responds dynamically to user inputs and includes audio generation. At the same time, the world model industry is beginning to consolidate. Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs is being acquired by AMD, Amazon is in talks to buy Decart, and Rivian just acquired Third Dimension to bring simulation capabilities in-house for self-driving testing.
Genie 4 is Google’s latest move to stay ahead in the crowded field.
Google released its predecessor, Genie 3, as a research preview a little over a year ago. Aside from being far more photorealistic and featuring audio, Genie 4 allows for free-form edits, like changing the weather or camera angle in real time or adding new people or objects. It can maintain a consistent scene for up to two minutes, double its predecessor’s limit, and offers better physics and more humanlike characters.
Gemini, Google’s AI model, is also more closely integrated with Genie 4, acting as the director that plans steps and checks frames while Genie creates the visuals. In a research experiment tied to Gemini Robotics, a Gemini 4 Argon model broke down tasks into steps that Genie 4 simulated in real time. The experiment shows a possible way to test robot scenarios in simulation before they happen in the real world.
“What we’ll increasingly see in the future are these hybrid world models, where you have a combination of Gemini writing code and text, and Genie ingesting that in real time and simulating reality at different levels of abstraction,” Tejas Kulkarni, research director at Google, said during a briefing.
As with other world models, the pitched commercial use cases include gaming, interactive learning, and robotics. One speculative example of interactive learning would be entering a painting of a historical scene and chatting to the painting’s subjects about the event portrayed.
But “trusted testers” — the people who get first access to Google’s cutting-edge products — are pointing to a possible new use: prototyping films.
“The real time aspect becomes most valuable in the areas where keeping a state of flow in the creativity space becomes incredibly useful,” Diego Rivas, a Google DeepMind engineer, said during a press briefing. “For example, in the ideation phase, in the storyboarding phase — anytime you’re kind of in need of rapid ideation.”
Google also offers Veo, its AI video-generation model that makes high-definition clips with built-in synchronized audio from text, image, or video prompts — a tool that has been growing in popularity among filmmakers.
Rivas added that users could, eventually, rely on Gemini Omni, a multimodal large language model that can generate video from images, audio, and text, to turn those prototypes into creative assets. Though those capabilities, he says, are still a ways off.
Throughout the briefing, Rivas stressed that it’s still early days for Genie 4 and that it’s not yet clear what the end-to-end product experience will be. The team also acknowledged that Genie 4 still has gaps: Details and objects can drift the longer a simulation runs, and they still haven’t quite figured out how to ensure the audio will be accurate and any in-world text will be legible.
Genie 4 is available now as a research preview for trusted testers. In the coming weeks, the model will roll out to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie, Google’s AI tool for generating interactive worlds from text or image prompts, and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

articles.title: Book vs clamshell foldable phones: which is better for your everyday needs? - Engadget
articles.text:
Book vs clamshell foldable phones: which is better for your everyday needs?
Both styles have their perks.
There are two main types of foldable phones, clamshell phones and book-style ones. Clamshell designs harken back to the early days of flip phones — compact, square devices that flip open from bottom to top to reveal a traditional bar-style phone. It's a popular throwback design with advantages like a glanceable front screen that old flip phones of yesteryear did not include (aside from small monochrome ones on models from the early 2000s). By contrast, book-style phones are just that, opening from right to left like a book to reveal a larger, tablet-sized screen inside for more immersive viewing, interaction and productivity. One is not better than the other. It simply comes down to your specific needs.
While you'll find models of both types among the best foldable phones, you can see in form factor alone that they are markedly different. They're also designed for very different everyday needs. Clamshell phones are ideal if you want a compact device with glanceable information on an outer screen. By contrast, book-style foldables are best suited for those who want to view content on a larger screen, more like a potential tablet replacement.
Why you'd use clamshell or book style
Back in the day, having a flip phone was "cool," and it sort of is again. Unlike old models that only had a single screen inside, the latest versions have an outer screen where you can see pertinent information like incoming messages and calls, time and date, weather, calendar details, and with some models, even more apps. The benefit is being able to access what you need without having to open the phone. It's great for reducing distractions and convenient access to information you need at-a-glance.
When you want a larger screen, flip it open from bottom to top to reveal the standard phone screen. From there, they operate like traditional phones, but with a hinge in the middle. Because of the smaller designs, they're easier to operate one-handed than book-style foldables. But you don't get more real estate than you would with a traditional bar phone.
By contrast, a book-style foldable phone is similar in size to a traditional bar phone when it's closed, albeit a bit thicker. It has a screen on the outside to access basics like messaging, notifications and apps, just as you would on a regular phone. But open it to reveal a larger, tablet-sized screen. This is ideal for consuming content, like videos, books and games, surfing the web, and more.
Book-style foldables are good for productivity, too, including working on the go with widescreen or split screen views, even drag and drop actions. They feel more premium as well, but they are also larger and bulkier. They can also be more delicate with more complex mechanical designs, so you'll need to handle them with extra care. Get a good foldable phone case that protects the hinge especially.
How to choose
Deciding between these types of foldable phones comes down to personal needs. There are pros and cons to using foldable phones in general. If you want something compact with glanceable information, a clamshell phone is perfect. If you want to watch videos or play games on the go and enjoy a more immersive experience, a book-style foldable makes more sense.
Both types of foldable phones offer special advantage with dual screens, like being able to use two-sided live translations or the outer camera to preview photos. Both can also function as their own stands, sitting upright or in a tented position for photos, video calls and more.
Book-style foldable phones are becoming more popular, with research indicating they may surpass clamshell phone shipments in 2026, especially with exciting new models like the Apple iPhone Duo (see our iPhone Duo hands-on). It's not just because you can do more on these larger devices, and we rely on our phones for so much. It's also because buyers are shifting towards premium products with more memory because of the memory shortage. Having one device with more memory that functions as both a phone and a tablet is an attractive proposition.
But book-style foldables also consume more battery since they have to power two large screens. They're the same size as a traditional phone when closed, usually a bit thicker. Clamshell phones are much smaller, but don't offer as much power and have less screen real estate. It comes down to what you prioritize most and how you want to use the device.

articles.title: Oracle bundles AI video tools and streaming into one media platform
articles.text:
Oracle announced Media Fabric at AI World, a platform that combines its own AI video and image models, an AI production suite and a live-streaming network. It lets brands make many versions of one ad. Oracle says it will be available within 12 months.
Oracle has announced Media Fabric, a platform that uses AI to help media firms, streaming services and brands make video and stream it. The company unveiled it on Tuesday at its AI World event in Las Vegas. Oracle plans to release it within 12 months.
“Creating content and delivering it to viewers were separate processes,” said Oracle chief executive Clay Magouyrk. “With Oracle Media Fabric, we’re bringing content creation and streaming together, using AI across the entire production and distribution workflow.”
The platform includes Oracle’s own AI models for making and editing video and images. They sit inside a tool called Creative Studio. It can also pick models from other firms for each task, based on cost, security and copyright risk.
A third part, Oracle Video Edge, streams big live events. It uses live data to send each viewer to the best server, so streams start fast and stay smooth when crowds peak.
Brands can turn one advert into many versions that follow their own rules, and broadcasters can tailor shows to different viewers. Oracle says it has safeguards to protect customers’ work and to cut the risk that AI output copies someone else’s. Such worries pushed ByteDance into a pact with Hollywood over its AI video tool in August.
Oracle says Media Fabric gives creators of all sizes tools once used only by the biggest streaming platforms. Netflix, for one, already uses generative AI to help viewers find shows.
The launch is one of several at AI World this week, including a deal to offer Cerebras AI computers and a $1B fund for partners.

articles.title: How to Hide Your Baby From the Government
articles.text:
At first blush, Kristin LaHargoue’s social media resembles that of many thirtysomething moms espousing aspirational lifestyles. To her 88,000-plus followers on Instagram, LaHargoue—a crunchy blonde living in central Utah—routinely posts her children, her husband, and herself traipsing around the globe on her account @veda.revival. There they are, standing before the Sagrada Familia, striking silly poses on a busy Tokyo street, or dancing beachside in the Philippines. In an April 2026 post soundtracked to a version of Taylor Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia,” LaHargoue wrote that she and her family have thus far traveled to over 40 countries.
Flying around the world at such a clip isn’t unusual for influencers. But LaHargoue says her children, although born in the US, travel without birth certificates or Social Security numbers. Her thinking is aligned with the sovereign citizen movement: an ever-expanding group of anti-government activists that, for almost half a century, have operated on the belief that they aren’t subject to US law. “Hot take: You don’t actually need a birth certificate to raise a thriving, traveling, fully functional child,” she writes in the same post. “Yeah … I said it. Because we are living proof of it.” By virtue of not registering her two young children’s births, she says her sons are “sovereign babies”—an oft-used hashtag, on accounts such as LaHargoue’s, to describe a child bearing alternative identification documents.
With her brand Veda Revival, LaHargoue offers a white-glove concierge service to new and expecting parents, rooted in the belief that obtaining requisite birth documents is tantamount to entering one’s children into “the jurisdiction of the US corporation.” A larger sovereign citizen movement has existed in the US for decades, with its practitioners similarly eschewing traditional government documents; acts of protest can also include tax evasion, driving without a license, and in the case of Terry Nichols—domestic terrorism. But the rise of influencers selling an alternative means of obtaining a passport, and the idea that babies can be sovereign, represents a new, digitally native outgrowth of this ideology.
For $497, LaHargoue sells a bundle that includes videos and templates for parents to obtain passports for their children based on “nationality” versus “citizenship,” with detailed instructions so they might respond confidently during “interactions with agents of the matrix.” Those seeking something more intensive can pay $997 for “hand-holding,” meaning that LaHargoue will personally guide them in navigating this divergent route. (LaHargoue declined WIRED’s request for an interview, citing the forthcoming birth of her third child.)
LaHargoue, who says she has worked with over 1,000 parents to obtain passports for their sovereign babies, is one of a growing cohort of influencers working in the unregulated industry that’s now selling this self-taught knowledge. One “family legacy architect” named Minister Dionne, known for broadcasting missives to her 125,000 Instagram followers about how registering one’s child makes them “wards of the state,” offers “Status Correction FastTrack Bundles” for securing noncitizen national passports (for as much as $555). LaHargoue also offers an affiliate program for those who want to make a commission of 15 to 20 percent by successfully selling her sovereign baby services.
It’s impossible to quantify how many sovereign babies currently live in the US, given their parents’ feelings about record-taking. (According to one oft-cited estimate, 100,000 to 300,000 people identify as sovereign citizens, although it's hard to know exactly because of the nature of the movement.) But Adam Bojak, a family law attorney in western New York who is currently on the ballot for the New York state legislature, says that he’s seen an uptick in cases involving sovereign children. In decades past, he’d have maybe one client per year who’d vacate or even try to reject formal identification documents for their children; lately, that’s increased to a half dozen a year, a phenomenon he suspects is linked to the “psychic break” that happened during Covid. “So many of these things are downstream from the aftereffects of that,” he says. “Just where people were ripped apart socially and physically from each other, emotionally. [It’s a rupture] that leads into this idea that everybody’s out for themselves.”
Remote learning during the pandemic also transformed education. Homeschooling rates surged in the early 2020s and remain high: The National Home Education Research Institute estimated earlier this year that 3.4 million children in the US are homeschooled—a number that is almost certainly underreported—compared to 1.4 million back in 2003. Tess Ulrey, executive director of the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, is unsurprised that the sovereign baby movement has risen in tandem with homeschooling rates, as homeschooling can become an inadvertent gateway into sovereign thinking. Some parents might pull their child out of school and “get tied up in this ideology of like, ‘Well, it is my right to do whatever I want. Well, why would the government be tracking that?’” she says.
Indeed, peppered between posts name-checking Rumi and denouncing circumcision, LaHargoue encourages parents to reject conventional education systems. In her July appearance on the Born Free Method podcast, LaHargoue spoke about her belief that the US school system is connected to a larger government plot that, by virtue of the birth certificate, “contracts” children as human capital. “That school system is now teaching them how to be a good worker,” she said. “Let’s shuffle them right down this path.”
A recent rise in “world schooling,” or rooting a child’s instruction in travel rather than curricula, is similarly linked with the sovereign baby movement. Jemila Moore, a doula based in South Carolina, lives nomadically with her partner and four young children. Her three youngest kids have neither birth certificates nor Social Security numbers. Moore, who swears by world schooling, wanted to ensure that her children had the ability to travel with passports. Wherever her family may be, Moore accompanies her children to local public libraries to read and do math exercises. “There's nothing greater than children being able to learn about other countries while actually witnessing those countries and their culture, and let those countries tell their history versus just reading it in a textbook,” she says. “I think that it really makes a difference on our development as people and how we view the world.”
While sovereign babies are bred on the grounds of government suspicion, sovereign-minded parents still “want to travel under the banner of the United States of America without actually being subject to the United States of America,” says Bojak. “Like George Costanza said, ‘We’re living in a society,’ and these are the barriers you have to clear to live in a society.” Rob Finch, a North Carolina–based consultant who trains law enforcement officers to engage with sovereign citizens who don’t believe they are subject to the law, says this ideology is "not fact-based," adding: “You've got a lot of opportunistic people selling these packages of ‘Keep your kid off the grid, here's how you do it.’”
Without clearing these barriers, experts worry that sovereign babies are far more likely to fall through societal cracks and live insular lives. Most will be unable to drive, find jobs, or even secure housing without the crucial documents one needs to move through the world.
Birth certificates and Social Security numbers represent a relatively new standard for identification in the US. During the colonial period, American churches primarily kept birth records. But when millions of Europeans immigrated to the States in the 19th century, reformers became concerned about rising poverty rates, overpopulation, and the spread of epidemics in densely populated urban areas. In a bid to better understand public health, the US Census Bureau developed standardized certificates and began tracking births, though not every state followed suit. The process became more nationally standardized around the 1930s, and firmly de rigueur during World War II, when some factories would only employ US citizens as part of the war effort.
To some sovereign citizens, it’s no coincidence that birth certificates became rote in the 1930s, the same decade FDR signed an executive order replacing gold as the backing standard for US currency. Proponents of the “straw man theory,” a central premise in sovereign ideology, hold that when parents take out a birth certificate and Social Security number for their child, the government then opens an account in their name and uses them, in the absence of gold, as human capital to back US debt. This bogus theory is often invoked by sovereign citizens who, say, get pulled over for driving without a license, as a way of justifying their actions: They believe that every individual has two separate personas—a legal entity that is bound by the government, and themselves—and that laws thus don’t apply to them as individuals. To date, no US court has ever sided with sovereign citizens invoking these arguments, says family law attorney Christopher C. Melcher: “There's no legal basis for what they're saying, but they say it with enough conviction and consistency that they hope they can get away with it.”
The modern sovereign citizens movement has its roots in a hate-fueled paramilitary cohort called Posse Comitatus (Latin for “power of the county”). In the 1970s, an ex-Army lieutenant colonel turned “minister” named William Potter Gale founded the group, hinged on racist and antisemetic beliefs, in Southern California. Gale believed in a “citizen’s government” that would exact justice in its own way; throughout the decade, his followers violently detained and assaulted an IRS worker and attempted to “indict” a judge. When an agricultural crisis gripped the US, his conspiracy-driven ideas spread throughout the country. Posse Comitatus’ anti-government tactics, which include not paying taxes, later spread into a larger sovereign citizens’ movement, which now has dozens of different factions and chapters in various states. One such group is the American State Nationals, who align with sovereign citizen ideology but distance themselves from the moniker because of the movement’s white supremacist origins. ASNs believe one can obtain a noncitizen national passport that, by virtue of having a certain number of stars on it, gives them limited diplomatic immunity. Some even sell bundles on social media that allow people, for several hundred dollars, to exit their “contract” with the US government through a passport based on nationality rather than citizenship.
Beyond a skepticism of the US government, the parents of sovereign babies are difficult to pin down. They typically do not align with any one political party or religious group. While some live more holistic and off-grid lifestyles, and an overlap does exist between sovereignty practitioners and ardent anti-vaxers, it wouldn’t be accurate to say that this is a strain of the Make America Healthy Again movement, either. Rather than having one centralized leader or a physical community, the sovereign baby phenomenon is more akin to a vast constellation, people connected by the belief that by applying for a birth certificate and Social Security number, they are “binding” their children with the “United States corporation,” as LaHargoue likes to put it. In a series of videos included in Veda Revival’s “Born Free Blueprint,” LaHargoue argues that sovereign babies are “ushering in a new era of freedom.” (These videos are free, but before purchasing and viewing LaHargoue’s more in-depth guides, all clients are required to upload a passport/ID and sign an agreement accepting the terms of entering her member community—which threatens legal action if one does not use her information with “integrity and benevolence.”)
The US Department of State requires evidence of citizenship before approving a passport. If one doesn’t have a primary document (such as a birth certificate), the agency accepts several forms of secondary evidence, including a delayed birth certificate and a Letter of No Record—which must be issued by the state and include public record documents such as a hospital birth certificate, baptism records, school records, or a census record. Those hewing to sovereign thinking tend to go with another option: a family Bible containing written inscriptions denoting the births and deaths of relatives. Melcher says it’s difficult, but not impossible, for those born on US soil to obtain secondary evidence that’s “sufficient to convince the State Department to issue a passport, based on them claiming that they were born in a state or territory, without a birth certificate.”
A woman living in Texas, whom I’ll call Deborah, purchased an instructional video from LaHargoue’s catalog and says she was able to obtain a passport for her infant—sans birth certificate—by submitting baptism records, a family Bible, an affidavit confirming that she had indeed given birth to him, and a formal announcement in a local newspaper announcing his birth. She notarized each of these documents and sent them certified through the mail. After an extensive back and forth, she said the office eventually approved the passport. “I opted for the passport route because that is a way of announcing, ‘Hey, I have this child,’” she says. “I'm claiming parental rights and backing them with the paperwork they'll need to make whatever choices they want in the future.”
In recent years, parents have stumbled into the sovereign baby movement through online rabbit holes, especially on Instagram, Telegram, Facebook, and Reddit. The confluence of factors that has given way to the sovereign baby movement—including the ubiquity of influencers, the isolating aftermath of Covid, skepticism of the medical establishment, and waning trust in the government—feels utterly of this time. Yet this phenomenon clashes against another tension: the Trump administration’s brutality toward immigrants and visible show of deporting people out of the US. At a moment when undocumented immigrants, green card holders, asylum seekers, and citizens are being shuttled to remote countries with little legal recourse, it’s striking that parents of sovereign children—of babies born in the US—have consciously stacked the odds against themselves and their kids.
“We shouldn't discount the fact that there's a guy in the Oval Office now, for the second time, who doesn't believe any rules pertain to him, and he's actually proven that over and over again that he doesn't have to follow laws,” Bojak, the attorney, says. “He doesn't have to follow court orders. And so if he doesn't, why the hell should any of the rest of us?”
Others arrive in other ways entirely: Deborah learned about sovereign citizen ideology—and later declined to get her toddler a birth certificate—after she’d accrued over $2,000 in speeding tickets. (She rejects the term "sovereign citizen” and claims it’s a slur; instead, she prefers to say she is "maximizing potential freedom” for her child.) “I ended up doing this deep dive from just having, honestly, a totally delusional idea of, ‘I'm not gonna pay these,’” she says. Some, like Zoe Durant, got here through in-person conversations with a doula, a midwife, or another professional birth attendant who usually helps new parents complete standard paperwork.
In 2016, while studying engineering in college, Durant was working as a bottle server and promotional model in Nevada. Several months after giving birth to her first child that same year, Durant and her partner traded the neon gleam of casinos for an offgrid solar farm mere miles away from Kilauea, one of the world’s most active volcanoes. She’s a “first-generation farmer” of grapefruits, bananas, lilikoi, and lychee crops in the remote Hawaiian jungle, posting dispatches on Instagram under the name @junglefairyfarm. (They have since moved to a less harsh location).
Early into building their Big Island home, in 2021, Durant found out she was pregnant with her second child. When she learned that her partner couldn’t accompany her to requisite appointments because of Covid, Durant eschewed a hospital birth altogether. Instead, she found a midwife who helped deliver her daughter in a birthing pool at home. When it was time to consider her newborn’s birth certificate and Social Security number application, Durant consulted her midwife. “She was like, ‘Well, there's families that I work with who don't do that,’” Durant says. “And I was like, ‘Oh, tell me more.’”
The midwife, Durant explained, told her that she’d helped several parents who identified as sovereign. Intrigued, and recalling how she’d felt pushed to sign these papers after her first child’s hospital birth, Durant chewed over the alternative the midwife had told her about. “It seems like something that [my daughter] could do later on if she wanted to consent to that, and it also helps protect her identity,” Durant reasoned. “In the future, she's not going to worry about someone stealing her Social Security number. And honestly, the way the economy is, I don't even know if Social Security is going to be around when she's old enough.”
But Durant worried that without documents like a birth certificate and a Social Security card, her child might run into hurdles if she wished to live a normal life. Durant instead applied for a passport for her daughter, submitting various secondary documents. At one point, Durant says, a passport agent told her that the office couldn’t grant her the document because she didn’t have hard proof of her child’s birth. Durant then sent the official a photo of herself sitting in the shallow birthing pool with her newborn, telling them, “This is the only evidence I have of the birth—because it was a sovereign birth.” These are “my beliefs,” she added, “sorry if you don’t like it.” She says the birth photo worked, and the passport office eventually sent the document along; all told, it took about six months.
Last year, Durant wrote and self-published a book, Opting Out: A Parent's Guide to a Barcode-Free Birth and Keeping Your Child Off the Grid: How to Protect Your Child's Identity and Secure Their Future Outside the State’s System. At a little under $20 per copy, it’s not the main source of the content creator/model’s income—she’s sold a few hundred copies thus far, she estimates—but Durant says that’s secondary to how “passionate” she feels about the subject. “I think a lot of parents are just trying to take back power because the government is getting a little bit overzealous with their control,” she says. One chapter of Durant’s book is dedicated solely to dealing with Child Protective Services, should the agency inquire about why one’s child does not have a birth certificate. In it, she writes: “Take a deep breath. Stand your ground. You have done your research. They were not taking your child. In that moment you realized something. The birth certificate was not just paperwork. It is permission, permission for the government to track you. To control you and intervene in your family's life whenever they see fit.”
Durant’s beliefs diverge from the mainstream sovereign baby movement, which is intertwined with free birthing—a separate, largely influencer-led movement that advocates for giving birth without medical intervention. In 2024, 1.5 percent of births in the US were free births, a number that tripled from 2004. (Durant had assistance during her home birth and believes in seeking out traditional medicine for “life-saving care”; she has been undergoing chemotherapy for a stage IV colon cancer diagnosis.) Free birthers can also opt out of prenatal care altogether, in what’s known as a “wild pregnancy.” LaHargoue, a vocal proponent of the Free Birth movement, has posted about her appearance on the Free Birth Society Podcast alongside Reels about traveling without these documents.
Marisse Vista, 34, first learned about sovereignty during the pandemic, when she was newly single and pregnant. She felt alone, save for an online “village of women” whom Vista credits with helping her “unearth a lot of things that didn't align with what I had known to be true.” After one woman told her that she believed “the birth certificate was a [government] bond,” Vista began questioning other “mainstream things,” like vaccinating her children. When Vista became pregnant with her second child, she decided to free-birth at an Airbnb after “binging” the FBS podcasts. After she decided not to obtain traditional birth documents for her infant, she started poking around online to find alternate routes to getting a passport.
By that point, Vista, a first-generation Filipina who grew up in Spring, Texas, had launched a Facebook community for like-minded sovereign mothers. When Vista mentioned in the group that she’d been trying to get her head around the alternative passport process, someone brought up Veda’s name. Vista bought LaHargoue’s step-by-step course to ensure that she had the requisite documents before going to the passport office in Waco. LaHargoue became her “echo chamber to make sure that I was doing it like fully right, because I had done all this research alone,” Vista says. “It was just a confirmation that, like, all my research was correct.”
When she became pregnant with her third child, Vista had “a pain-free, orgasmic, Frank breech free birth,” meaning that the baby emerges from the birth canal buttocks-first. The experience led Vista to help people conceive their “spirit babies” and birth them as sovereign parents. Under the banner of her brand La Souveraine Mere, her services range from a digital guide to “understanding how spirit babies communicate, what they need energetically before they can land, and how to align your womb space with their frequency” ($44) to a “Sovereign Conception Program” that includes “Spinal Energetics, frequency work, ancestral clearing, and womb activation woven into a container that treats your body as the oracle it already is” ($5,555).
Once these expectant parents get into Vista’s “world,” as she describes, “then I start to talk about, like, ‘Once you have the baby, what are you going to do? You're going to steward them. You're going to make sure that … their custodian isn't the government,’ and so we then talk about birth certificates and Social Security numbers.”
A bone-deep distrust of the medical establishment—and, in some cases, traumatic experiences—is another common gateway into free-birthing and, then, the sovereign baby movement. Moore, the former nursing assistant who studied public health in college, says she wasn’t expecting to feel “very pressured” to get an induction until she went into labor at a hospital. “When I was like, ‘Hey, since I'm already contracting, can we not do the induction? Can I just let my body go naturally?’” she says. “They're like, ‘Well, the doctor put the order in. We're just gonna do it.’” In hindsight, Moore wishes she had "advocated for herself more” in that moment. “My body was probably already doing what was necessary for me, and the induction just made my labor process a little bit more challenging than what it is actually with the natural flow.” Moore says it caused her to reflect on the disparities that women of color face when delivering children, and later informed her decision to free-birth her other kids.
There is an indisputable maternal health crisis in this country, and especially among women of color. But experts warn that free-birthing carries a heightened risk of complications, and the practice has come under intense scrutiny after infants and parents alike have died from the complications of unassisted birth. Sovereign baby influencers may risk further sowing distrust by advocating for risky, radical procedures without any prenatal care or medical professionals—particularly to those who might already be more vulnerable—by alleging that physicians are cogs in a bigger birth-certificate conspiracy. “They’ve tricked us into hiring licensed providers,” LaHargoue says in a video titled “Who’s Child Is It Really? The Truth About Birth Certificates & Legal Fiction.” “They’ve tricked us into believing that birth is even a medical event.”
“I’ve been saving this cigarette,” Sarah Ashley Townsend tells me over Zoom one June afternoon. She’s sitting in her home in Maryland, near the Susquehanna River. The windows are open. “I think that’s the hardest part to talk about,” the 43-year-old says, lighting the end of the smoke. Townsend is referring to the moment she became aware that she’d been raised differently.
Shortly before her birth, Townsend’s mother tumbled down the sovereign-ideology-aligned rabbit hole via a neighbor, who convinced her to not give birth at a hospital and to refuse paperwork. “I was not given a Social Security number, because she was going to do this all outside the boundaries of society now,” Townsend says. Vaccines were verboten, and she and her siblings lived consciously isolated from others in their community.
When her father’s family intervened and lobbied to send Townsend to school, the 5-year-old walked into kindergarten “thinking that I started school with everyone else, and I did not,” she says, her voice breaking. “I thought it was the first day of school, and apparently it was the last month of school. They made fun of me because I couldn't tie my shoes … and they all asked if I was from another planet.” Townsend’s mother would pack her inappropriate lunches or fight over signing papers that would have allowed her child to buy a meal: “She didn’t want me to have their tainted food,” she says. “She would blame us for subscribing to their system, because she didn't think we should have to be there anyway.”
Townsend considers herself fortunate that her father, while distant, advocated for her. One day he showed up at Townsend’s elementary school, and the pair walked to a medical clinic; he quietly ensured that she received vaccinations without her mother knowing. After her parents divorced, Townsend’s mother moved her and her sister around constantly, choosing off-grid places where they sometimes lived without power for months. Townsend’s father would ship her boxes with plushies and gift cards hidden inside, which she would use to buy clothes. Her dad would tuck novels into these packages with words underlined, a secret code telling her she was loved, and that she needed to stay strong.
When Townsend was 16, she tried to apply for a driver’s license and was repeatedly denied on account of her inconsistent birth and medical history. She approached her music and theater teachers for help: “How do I be an adult … how do I go do things I'm supposed to do?” she remembers asking them.
She believed she had her documents straightened out by the time she turned 18. But Townsend kept running into hurdles when she tried to join her husband’s health insurance shortly afterward. Giving birth a year later became its own kind of hell. “Do you know what happened when I gave birth to my son? All of his paperwork got kicked back,” she says, because the office said it couldn’t find evidence of her own birth. “My son's birth certificate had to be amended twice. I'm a week postpartum, 22 years old, running all over town with my husband getting notarized documents,” she says. “All I want is for my kid to have … of all the things in the world, a Social Security number and a birth certificate from the get-go.”
More than two decades on, Townsend is still haunted because she lacked a birth certificate and a Social Security number earlier in life. “As an adult, you can't have a fucking normal existence, ever, because you always have to go through a routine that will remind you that no one cared, and that you were some pawn in a weird fucking game that will affect you for the rest of your life,” she says. “And like, yes, I'm a valid citizen. I live here. I am a person. I exist.”

articles.title: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
articles.text:
Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms of service before the recent slowdown, as reported earlier by Ars Technica. According to Musk, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” however Ukrainian officials have denied that happened, or that it is actually possible for them to do.
Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
Musk accuses Ukraine’s military of using Starlink to carry out drone strikes, which officials have denied.
The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of putting limits on the military’s satellite internet service that disrupted its drone missions and operations. As reported by Axios, Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and to defend against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say that Ukraine uses Starshield, the US military-controlled variant of Starlink.
Musk points to a post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which said Ukraine uses “Starlink from mid-range strikes against enemy military targets,” in violation of Starlink’s policies. However, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, pushed back on this in a post on Telegram, saying Starlink’s systems can only connect to devices traveling between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour (around 43 and 55 miles per hour) and don’t work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Ars Technica also points out a tweet from another former Ukrainian advisor, Serhii Sternenko, that went into more detail, saying that while stationary terminals could be registered (with Starlink) by military personnel or civilians, “for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system… In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. With the restriction lifted, Ukraine’s military can now connect to devices traveling at speeds of more than 400km/h (248mph), the Kyiv Independent reports.
Though Musk initially offloaded the blame for the slowdown in Ukraine onto the US government, President Donald Trump responded by saying he “wasn’t involved” and didn’t know who throttled SpaceX’s services. A report from The Wall Street Journal later said Trump asked Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine.

articles.title: Exclusive: Meta director Rohit Patel departs after 8 years to take on Microsoft Office Suite
articles.text:
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc, a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.
Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, AI researcher Andrew Tulloch, and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith.
Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.
Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.
The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents.
“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”
In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.
Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models.
“I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.”
Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.
His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.”
Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.”
Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.
OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, SpaceXAI, and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.
Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.
“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”
There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.
“My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.”
Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.
As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.
For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.
“Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.”

articles.title: Lãi suất ngân hàng hôm nay 27/10: Các kỳ hạn có lãi suất từ 7%/năm trở lên
articles.text:
Tính đến ngày 27/10, theo biểu lãi suất được khảo sát, không còn nhiều ngân hàng niêm yết lãi suất trên 7%/năm, trong số này có MBV, PGBank, Saigonbank, Sacombank, VCBNeo, VIB và VPBank.
Saigonbank sau khi giảm lãi suất tiền gửi từ ngày 23/10 đã đưa lãi suất về dưới ngưỡng 7%/năm ở hầu hết kỳ hạn tiền gửi, ngoại trừ kỳ hạn 13 tháng vẫn được niêm yết ở mức 7,9%/năm.
Mức lãi suất huy động cao nhất tại VPBank là 7,4%/năm, áp dụng cho các kỳ hạn từ 15-18 tháng. Trong khi đó, lãi suất niêm yết cho kỳ hạn 24 tháng là 7,1%/năm.
Ở các kỳ hạn còn lại, lãi suất niêm yết của VPBank đều dưới 7%/năm sau khi ngân hàng điều chỉnh giảm vào đầu tuần này.
Sau đợt điều chỉnh, mức lãi suất cao nhất tại Sacombank giảm từ 7,8% xuống 7,3%/năm, áp dụng cho tiền gửi kỳ hạn 24-36 tháng từ 500 triệu đồng.
Tuy nhiên, mức lãi suất này chỉ được áp dụng cho các khoản tiền gửi từ 500 triệu đồng. Cũng với mức tiền gửi này, Sacombank niêm yết lãi suất tiền gửi 7%/năm cho kỳ hạn 12-18 tháng.
Lãi suất tiết kiệm 7%/năm cũng được Sacombank niêm yết cho kỳ hạn 24-36 tháng đối với các khoản tiền gửi từ 50 triệu đồng đến dưới 500 triệu đồng, trong khi lãi suất áp dụng cho khoản tiền gửi dưới 50 triệu đồng đều đã về dưới 7%/năm.
Ngân hàng chuyển giao bắt buộc VCBNeo niêm yết lãi suất 7%/năm cho tiền gửi kỳ hạn từ 6-36 tháng. Một ngân hàng chuyển giao bắt buộc khác là MBV đang niêm yết lãi suất 7%/năm cho các kỳ hạn từ 7-36 tháng.
Tại VIB, mức lãi suất huy động 7%/năm đang được niêm yết cho kỳ hạn 12 tháng. Đây cũng là mức lãi suất đang được PGBank niêm yết cho hai kỳ hạn 12 và 13 tháng.
Ngoài mức lãi suất tiết kiệm cao nhất được niêm yết tại các ngân hàng nói trên, lãi suất tiết kiệm thực tế còn vượt ngưỡng 8%/năm tại một số ngân hàng bằng các chính sách cộng thêm lãi suất.
Ngân hàng Nhà nước yêu cầu các ngân hàng triển khai việc giảm lãi suất huy động và cho vay trên toàn hệ thống, ở tất cả các kênh bán hàng.
Cơ quan quản lý cũng yêu cầu các ngân hàng giảm tối thiểu 0,5 điểm phần trăm đối với lãi suất tiền gửi bình quân của các giao dịch phát sinh mới, ở các kỳ hạn từ 6 tháng trở lên, trong những tháng cuối năm 2026 so với mức lãi suất của chính ngân hàng trong kỳ báo cáo từ ngày 11 đến 20/10/2026.
NHNN cho biết sẽ theo dõi số liệu lãi suất bình quân của các giao dịch phát sinh mới trong những tháng cuối năm thông qua hệ thống báo cáo thống kê. Trường hợp ngân hàng không thực hiện theo yêu cầu, cơ quan này có thể áp dụng biện pháp xử lý, trong đó có việc xem xét điều chỉnh chỉ tiêu tăng trưởng tín dụng.
