articles.title: I Want Better Tap Water. Is Reverse Osmosis the Answer?
articles.text:
That funny taste in your tap water may be a harmless nuisance—or it may be cause for serious concern. Either way, you can do something about it by installing a reverse osmosis (RO) water filtration system in your home.
Stand-alone RO systems and pitchers sit on your countertop and generally require manual refilling from the tap. You’ll save space and avoid the hassle of constantly refilling the unit by installing an under-sink or under-counter model that connects directly to your plumbing lines. Either way, RO systems aren’t cheap. But for some homeowners, they may be an invaluable investment.
Featured in this Article
What Is Reverse Osmosis?
Osmosis is the movement of molecules—usually water—through a semipermeable membrane that blocks larger particles like salts and sugars from passing through. After osmosis, the concentration of particles on both sides of the membrane ends up in equilibrium. It’s how plants get water from the soil, and it’s how your kidneys filter junk out of your blood.
While osmosis is a spontaneous phenomenon that happens naturally, reverse osmosis requires pressure to force water through a membrane in the other direction, effectively removing all of those compounds from the water to render it pure. It’s how salt is removed from seawater to make it drinkable, and it’s one way tap water can be purified in your home.
RO differs considerably from traditional filtration systems, which rely on physical barriers, typically activated carbon, to manually capture particles that pass through. Eventually, these filters become saturated with sediments and other matter and have to be replaced. While carbon filters are fairly blunt, able to capture larger particles of at least 0.1 microns in size, RO systems have a much finer-grained membrane that captures contaminants on a microscopic level (typically down to 0.0001 microns).
Carbon filters can make your water taste and smell better, but with RO you are getting much, much cleaner water than what that inexpensive Brita filter can muster. (That said, RO can’t capture everything, and carbon filters are still useful for capturing certain volatile organic compounds through adsorption. Most RO systems also have an additional carbon filtration system included.)
Note that two types of RO systems are available: Tanked RO systems filter water slowly (albeit passively, without electricity) and sequester it in a (rather large) tank under your sink. Today, tankless RO systems are more popular, processing water on demand but requiring electricity to keep things flowing expeditiously. Tankless systems are considerably more expensive due to their inherent complexity.
What Are the Real Risks of Contaminants in Water Today?
“US tap water is safe for most people most of the time,” says John Voll, an industrial water treatment veteran and the founder of Tap & Air, a website that monitors water and air quality for hundreds of municipalities. “The problems are local, not universal.”
The first step to understanding your personal risk is to gauge whether your own water is up to snuff by simply looking up its most recent data report online. The Safe Drinking Water Act requires community water systems to publish an annual report on the quality of water they’re delivering, due by July 1 each year.
These are heady documents, so to keep things simple, Voll says to keep your eye on three key pollutant metrics: lead, nitrate or arsenic, and PFAS (so-called forever chemicals popular in nonstick cookware and other products). While the first two are serious issues, they’re fairly rare today. PFAS, however, are a particularly significant problem across the country. Voll says that 98 of the 200 largest US cities have at least one PFAS compound detected in their water supply. Reverse osmosis systems can handle them—as well as lead and other compounds. Carbon filters usually can’t.
“Most people don't need RO,” Voll says, “but some households clearly do, and the way to tell is to read your own water report first.”
What Are the Drawbacks of Using an RO System?
RO systems come with a host of downsides, but most are related in some fashion to cost.
- RO wastes water: The particulars of RO technology have historically meant it requires a large amount of unprocessed tap water to create a small amount of purified water, sometimes up to 4 gallons or more of tap to 1 gallon of clean water (called the pure-to-drain ratio). In recent years that number has dramatically shifted, with 4 gallons of tap water producing up to 3 gallons of clean water, or a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio.
- Filters are costly: RO systems can require up to six different filtration cartridges that must be replaced every year or two, depending on use. Much like printer ink, these costs can be easily overlooked when making your initial purchase. Plan to spend $50 to $200 annually on replacement cartridges, but check prices before you buy.
- RO can strip “good” minerals from your water: Calcium, magnesium, and potassium are all unable to pass through the RO membrane. RO systems also remove fluoride from your water, which many users may not desire and which dentists abhor. Some RO systems can remineralize water and/or raise the pH level of the processed water thanks to additional cartridges—but these, of course, mean further expense on replaceables.
- Plan for professional installation (and additional financial outlays): I try not to DIY too much when there’s even a remote potential for a water leak, so I get a plumber involved for installations like these. And since most RO systems require their own faucet, you’ll need to prepare to have a new hole drilled into your countertop for your tap if you don’t already have one available.
Do You Need an Under-Sink RO System?
Based on my analysis of my city’s water report, no I don’t really need an RO system, as there’s nothing hazardous to worry about. However, as the linked report notes, our water supplier uses chloramine as a disinfectant, and drinking that chloramine-treated water straight from the tap has a slight but noticeable, off-putting taste. This is exacerbated by the extreme hardness of the water; this part of Texas is basically built on top of nothing but limestone, and the resulting amount of calcium carbonate in the water can add a slightly bitter flavor, as well.
For me, RO is all about the way the water tastes. Any lingering contaminants that are removed along the way are just a bonus.
I tested the Waterdrop X12 for this story, hiring a plumber to remove a well-aged unit under the sink and replace it with this more capable one. The job was done in less than an hour.
Under-sink RO filters are separate from your existing plumbing, and most use three color-coded lengths of tubing to tie into it. One connects to your incoming water supply through an adapter valve, one clips into your wastewater drainpipe via an included fitting, and one connects to the faucet. I am confident I could have made these connections on my own—especially since I was replacing an existing system—but I’ve seen how even a small water leak can lead to devastating problems and was happy for the peace of mind that professional oversight supplied.
Once installed and powered up, the X12 launches a 35-minute priming process designed to flush the filters before first use. It seems like an awfully long time for the sink to run, and it is. If you have some way to capture and use all this extra water, plan ahead to collect it. After the session completed (it stops automatically), I was ready to start sipping from the tap.
The X12 is exceedingly simple to use. Tap the LED-equipped button on top of the faucet to start or stop the flow of water, or twist the same button to dial in the number of ounces you want to dispense (up to 999) before depressing it. This way, you can drop your 64-ounce Stanley Quencher in the sink and walk away without having to wait around or worry about an overflow, with a digital timer first offering a measurement of your water’s current TDS (total dissolved solids), then counting down the ounces as they’re dispensed. The good news is that you won’t have to wait long: The X12 blasts water out of its spigot faster than my kitchen sink does—a far cry from the sad dribble of H2O my old RO system provided.
The unit can also be switched into one of two alternate operating modes, including an energy-saving mode (which quiets the device) and “flow mode,” which is designed for high-use households. Both require pressing certain button combinations on the filtration unit. I have used the device in all three modes, and (contrary to other reviews I’ve seen) I’ve never found it to be noisy at all, even though it’s located just 20 feet from my bed.
As for the water, it tastes great. The remineralization feature and pH adjustment (to about 7.5, which I confirmed with a pH test strip) give the water a pleasant tang while avoiding any harshness or chemical flavors. Unfortunately it doesn’t come out particularly cold, which means having to add non-RO ice to the glass to chill it down. First-world problem, I know.
I was especially pleased to discover that the X12 has one of the best water efficiency rates in the business, with a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio (3 gallons of pure water production to 1 gallon lost). Replacement filters (three are needed in total) are sold à la carte for $30 to $160 each.
For an even more powerful version—ideal for larger households—consider the Waterdrop X16, which uses the same cartridges and offers the same features as the X12. WIRED editor Kat Merck, whose municipal water supply does contain PFAS, has had one installed for a year and a half without any maintenance or reliability issues.

articles.title: ASM lifts its 2027 sales forecast by a quarter as AI chipmakers spend
articles.text:
ASM International raised its 2027 revenue forecast to more than €5.7B, from above €4.6B, as memory and AI chipmakers expand. That reaches its 2030 target three years early. Third-quarter revenue rose 44% to a record €1.16B, and ASM plans a buyback of up to €300M.
ASM International has raised its 2027 sales forecast by about 24% as companies building AI data centres drive demand for chips, Bloomberg reported. The Dutch chip-equipment maker now expects revenue of more than €5.7B next year, up from above €4.6B forecast in July.
That puts ASM on track to hit its 2030 sales goal three years early, the company said on Tuesday. It also plans to buy back up to €300M of its shares.
ASM makes machines that lay down very thin layers of material on silicon wafers, a key step in making chips. Demand is coming from memory makers and from firms producing advanced chips for AI. It is one of several European firms profiting from the AI boom by selling tools rather than building AI models.
“Capacity remains tight across our customer base, and customers are moving quickly to increase output,” said chief executive Hichem M’Saad.
Third-quarter revenue rose 44% at constant currencies to a record €1.16B, while net income fell to €308.1M. Both beat analysts’ estimates. ASM’s US-listed shares rose 6.7% on Tuesday.
Its customers include TSMC, which plans to spend up to $64B this year after a sixth straight record profit, and Intel. ASM warned that its own supply chain is “stretched,” but said it is working with suppliers and customers to ship faster.
Fellow Dutch toolmaker ASML said this month that it cannot meet demand in 2027 or 2028 at current output levels.

articles.title: 20 Years of MacBook: How Apple shaped the laptops we use today - Engadget
articles.text:
20 Years of MacBook: How Apple shaped the laptops we use today
Apple has influenced everything from unibody laptop cases to high-res screens.
The dream of a truly portable Mac is almost as old as the Macintosh itself. Five years after the debut of the original Macintosh desktop in 1984, Apple launched the disastrously expensive, 16-pound Macintosh Portable. It failed quickly. But out of the ashes came the PowerBook 100 in 1991, followed by the more refined PowerBook 500 and PowerBook G3 in 1994. Apple finally struck mainstream consumer gold with the colorful iBook G3 in 1999. With a small handle and an adorably rounded case, what more could you want? It wasn't exactly fast, but it was a clear sign that Apple was aiming to make computers that appeal to the masses.
I can remember the exact moment I first fell in love with an Apple laptop. It was right as I was entering college in 2001: I came in with a desktop I built myself, but I couldn't help but notice the gorgeous PowerBook G4 several classmates had. I adored its sleek titanium case and the way Mac OS X seemed lightyears beyond Windows XP. Then Apple announced the first MacBook Pro in 2006, improving on the PowerBook G4 in every way, and the computing world hasn't been the same since.
No matter what you think of Apple or its hardware, there's no doubt that MacBooks have been the defining laptops of the last two decades. PC makers rushed to ape the MacBook Pro's sleek unibody design, and the introduction of the MacBook Air spurred on the creation of ultraportable laptops.
Sure, Apple has had its missteps — the first MacBook Air was way too slow, and it later made the boneheaded decision to remove crucial ports from the MacBook Pro — but even those served as learning lessons for the PC industry.
2006: The MacBook, MacBook Pro and Apple's entry into Intel CPUs
One of the first major stories Engadget covered back in 2005 was Apple's switch to Intel CPUs, moving away from the PowerPC chips it relied on for years. That made the first MacBook Pro and MacBook, as well as the revamped iMac, pretty intriguing systems when they arrived in 2006. They weren't just spiffy new Macs, they were a sign that Apple was now directly competing with PCs using the exact same Intel Core Duo chips.
For the most part, the MacBook Pro and MacBook were yet another sign of Apple's design prowess, and a warning to the entire PC industry. The MacBook Pro was a slimmer and more refined version of the PowerBook G4's aluminum case, while the PowerBook carried over a similar aesthetic to a plastic frame. At the time, most PC makers focused on less exciting and more utilitarian designs. Sony was the rare PC company actually leaning into a premium aesthetic with its VAIO systems, but they were also notoriously slow and expensive.
2008: The unibody MacBook Pro and MacBook Air
In 2008, Apple debuted the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air which both featured "unibody" cases carved out from a single block of aluminum. And really, the PC industry has never been the same since. Apple's unibody cases were stronger, lighter and more attractive than anything we'd seen on mainstream laptops at that point, and the company has continued to evolve that concept over the last two decades.
PC makers struggled to replicate unibody cases for years — mainly, because Apple had a stranglehold on the global metal chassis supply chain. But eventually, Razer was able to get close with its 2011 Blade gaming laptop. Intel's push for ultraportable "Ultrabooks" in the early 2010s also led to other PC makers following suit. Dell's first XPS 13 combined an aluminum case and carbon fiber palm rests, while HP covered its Envy 14 laptop in Gorilla Glass to stand out.
Apple's first redesign of the 11-inch and 13-inch MacBook Air, which debuted in late 2010, also set a new standard for laptop shapes. Instead of simply being thin, they were slightly wedge-shaped, which gave them more room for larger batteries and faster SSD storage drives. Both ASUS and Acer took clear inspiration from the MacBook Air for all of their ultraportables throughout the 2010s.
2012: MacBook Pro with Retina Displays
With the 2012 MacBook Pro, Apple brought over the "Retina Display" concept it originally debuted on the iPhone 4. It features a resolution that's so sharp you can't discern individual pixels. The Retina Display MacBook Pro started a new trend towards high-resolution laptops. It wasn't long before every PC maker started racing to shove in better screen technology and more pixels into their systems. Ironically, Dell pioneered the razor-thin screen bezel design in the PC world, and it took Apple nearly a decade to seriously shave down its screen bezels.
2016: MacBook Pro complete redesign with Touch Bar
The 2016 MacBook Pro was a significant change for several reasons: It was the introduction of the Touch Bar, and Apple also removed all legacy ports, leaving it with only four USB-C ports and a headphone connection. Apple basically double-downed on the design of the 12-inch MacBook, which was notorious for having just a single USB-C port. (The company also released the MacBook Pro without a Touch Bar in 2016, which only had two USB-C ports and a headphone jack.) This redesign made the MacBook Pro lighter and thinner than ever before, but it also left many professionals out in the cold, since it didn't have a built-in SD card reader, Type-A USB ports or an HDMI connection. There wasn't even a dedicated MagSafe power port. The 2016 MacBook Pro was the peak of Apple designer Jony Ive's minimalist style, which often came at the cost of practicality.
The MacBook Pro's Touch Bar was divisive from the beginning, and aside from ASUS — which experimented with trackpad screens and is still exploring dual screens with the ZenBook Duo — few PC companies tried to compete. But Apple's decision to strip down ports gave PC makers permission to do the same, as we saw in premium systems like the XPS 13, HP Spectre and Microsoft Surface laptops after 2016. ASUS, Acer and others eventually started squeezing more legacy ports into their laptops, both as a response to consumer criticisms and a way to differentiate from Apple's limitations.
2020 and beyond: Apple Silicon, and a return to functional ports
In 2020, Apple completely reshaped its computers around its own M1 chip, an Arm-based system-on-a-chip that proved to be both more powerful and more efficient than Intel's x86 CPUs. Crucially, Apple Silicon brought together CPU cores, GPU cores, RAM, AI NPUs and I/O connections onto a single chip. The M1 MacBook Air and MacBook Pro were a revelation: They were incredibly fast, offered a huge battery boost and you couldn't even tell they were running emulated apps. While we'd seen Windows PCs dabble with Arm support over the years prior to 2020, they were always slow and offered terrible legacy support. Apple Silicon, and the company's reworked OS, demonstrated a far better way to build an Arm-based laptop.
Apple followed up with the redesigned M1 Pro and M1 Max MacBook Pro models in 2021, which finally brought back an SD card reader and HDMI port, as well as the M2 MacBook Air in 2022 (which I called a "near perfect" computer at the time). As a response, Microsoft rallied its partner Qualcomm to help build Copilot+ laptops, Arm-powered systems that could offer comparable battery life and performance to Apple's hardware. While the Copilot+ branding wasn't hugely successful, it at least helped to spur on better hardware in Windows laptops.
NVIDIA's RTX Spark system-on-a-chip, which powers new high-end AI-focused systems like the Surface Laptop Ultra and ASUS ProArt P16, is an attempt at delivering the high-end of Apple Silicon performance. RTX Spark systems are incredibly expensive, starting at $2,600 and scaling upwards of $7,000, but the platform's combination of a powerful GPU and up to 128GB of unified RAM makes it a compelling option for AI researchers.

articles.title: Whop raises $200M at $5.1B valuation after shipping three products in three months
articles.text:
Palo Alto-based Whop has closed a $200 million Series D led by Sequoia Capital and Shopify Ventures at a $5.1 billion valuation, and plans to open offices in Europe and Colombia, Bloomberg reported.
2The company said the capital will fund its expansion abroad and research into payments and advertising. Tether invested $200 million in Whop in February at a $1.6 billion valuation, which means the company’s valuation has more than tripled in eight months.
Whop describes its customers as business operators, from product chiefs at high-growth startups to 16-year-olds running their first business. It gives them a gamified interface and an extensive API for distribution, business creation and money. The company says roughly 25,000 operators generate $550 million a month on the platform, with more than 50,000 other people earning monthly from services to those businesses. Cumulative on-platform transactions have passed $7 billion across 185 countries.
That API can be driven by AI agents through the Whop CLI, released in July, which lets operators run their businesses via prompts. The CLI and the company’s MCP connectors handle 350,000-plus calls per day, and monthly active users top 14,700, according to the announcement. Whop has also launched Business Blueprints, which deploys a ready-to-sell business in a few clicks and has produced more than 21,000 businesses in six weeks, and Economic Intelligence, which recommends the highest-ROI next move for a business based on millions of past transactions. Economic Intelligence is paid for with an extra percentage of the revenue a business earns from using it.
In its announcement, Whop pointed to a Forbes report that entry-level job opportunities are at an all-time low and said AI is calling traditional career paths into question. The company pitches itself as a way for people to earn on their own terms, and says most businesses on it serve hyper-specific customer needs, citing neobanks for dropshippers, private jet booking platforms, invoicing software for trucking companies, data suppliers for humanoid robotics companies and emergency tree removal services.
“We take inspiration from the traditional economy in designing Whop, and because businesses are the primary conduit by which people earn money and create value, we focus on them as our primary customer,” said Steven Schwartz, co-founder and CEO.
Sequoia partner Doug Leone joins the board as part of the deal, per Bloomberg. “They’re doing about a half billion revenue, business is doing great, and we’re helping humanity create businesses for people who can’t find a job,” he said in the announcement.
Whop’s annualized run-rate revenue recently went past $400 million, from $60 million at the beginning of 2025, Bloomberg reported. Schwartz told the outlet that most revenue is a percentage of each transaction processed on the platform, with a blended average fee of about 6%. Its three founders, who met as teenagers over software that tracked sneaker releases, started the company in 2021; it employs around 110 people and has an office in New York.
Earlier investors include A*, Peter Thiel, Insight Partners and Bain Capital Ventures, per Bloomberg.
Whop is hiring for engineering, product, sales and operations roles.

articles.title: Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
articles.text:
In its latest gift to oil and gas companies, the Trump administration is expected to announce plans today to weaken rules that guard against methane leaks.
Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane
The Environmental Protection Agency is lowering standards meant to keep methane from leaking from oil and gas infrastructure.
Methane is a smog-forming pollutant and a powerful greenhouse gas that’s up to 80 times as potent as carbon dioxide on a 20-year horizon. It’s the primary component of what the fossil fuel industry calls “natural gas” that routinely leaks from oil and gas wells and pipelines.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is reversing course on its previous efforts to plug those leaks. As part of President Donald Trump’s deregulatory agenda, the EPA plans to undo Biden-era rules that were expected to cut methane emissions by 80 percent over 14 years.
Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming
The EPA teased the rule change earlier this month, saying in a press release that it was “days away” from making the proposal. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin says the rollbacks will save oil and gas companies $45 billion, while the previous rules would have incurred $18 billion in regulatory costs.
“This proposal takes on many of the problems American [oil and gas] producers and operators have raised with us,” Zeldin said in the October 7th press release. “The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the U.S. can reach its full energy potential.”
The agency is expected to step back standards for so-called “marginal wells” — old wells that produce little fuel but create an outsize amount of methane pollution from leaks. These wells are responsible for half of the industry’s methane emissions despite only producing 6 percent of US oil and gas, ProPublica reports. The EPA is also expected to end the Super Emitter Program that notified oil and gas infrastructure operators of large releases of methane reaching 100 kilograms per hour or more.
Trump plans to make the announcement from a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, today, Bloomberg reports. Not only is Texas the top oil- and gas-producing state in the US, it’s also the world’s biggest data center market. With more data center capacity under construction than any other state, Texas has become emblematic of the challenges energy-intensive AI models pose. In just five years, data centers could undo decades of air quality improvements in Texas, according to a recent report by the Houston Advanced Research Center.
Methane has caused about 30 percent of global warming so far. But unlike carbon dioxide, which can linger in the atmosphere for hundreds or thousands of years, methane dissipates in a little over a decade. That makes eliminating methane emissions, particularly from unintentional leaks, one of the fastest and most straightforward ways to stop global temperatures from rising.
The EPA’s rollbacks quickly triggered furor from health and environmental advocates. “Any proposed rollback to the federal methane rule is a slap in the face to families who are exposed to oil and gas pollution where they live, work, and play,” Celerah Hewes, a senior manager for state field campaigns at Moms Clean Air Force, said in an email ahead of the expected announcement. “For over a decade, [our group] has been fighting for methane protections for our families—and we were making progress. Today’s announcement from EPA is a massive blow to the efforts to safeguard our children’s health and our climate.”
The Biden-era methane rules were estimated to bring in up to $98 billion in benefits by reducing climate risks and health costs from air pollution, even after factoring in the costs of compliance. Plugging leaks was supposed to lead to up to $13 billion worth of recovered natural gas.

articles.title: Ford Fathom will be the cheapest American EV capable of powering a house | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Ford announced two new EV chargers today that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid.
The new chargers promise to be about half the cost of Ford’s existing equivalent products, which could make the technology available to more households. Ford said the Fathom itself will start at $28,350.
The Fathom will be capable of delivering “over 10 kW” to a home, Ford said. That would allow the electric vehicle to substitute for a small standby generator. For most U.S. homes, it wouldn’t be enough to power everything, but it could keep a refrigerator and air conditioner operational for about half a day.
Such capability has been touted as an advantage EVs have over fossil fuel vehicles, but not many EVs come properly equipped, and the chargers required to make use of vehicle-to-everything (V2X) services tend to be costly.
Ford’s two devices offer similar but differing capabilities.
The Home Power Station device can help customers shave their utility bill by charging the Fathom when power prices are low and sending electricity back to the home when prices are high. The automaker says it will cost around $650, about 50% less than its first-generation bidirectional charger.
The other option, Home Backup Power, is a package that bundles the Home Power Station with a second device, the Home Backup Panel, to allow the Fathom to also power parts or all of a home when the power goes out. Ford says the package will cost around $2,100, about 60% less than its first-generation product.
None of those prices include installation, which for existing V2X chargers can run up to $10,000, depending on how much electrical work needs to be done to prepare the home. Ford did not announce any partnerships with installers, though a spokesperson told TechCrunch that Ford would release more details at a later date.
Which loads the Fathom can power will vary by household and the specifics of each installation. Things like air conditioners and refrigerators, for example, typically require a large surge of power to start up, after which point their load drops. So-called soft-start devices can help mitigate the surge, though they add cost to the installation.
Both chargers will allow Fathom customers to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs), which use software to control a fleet of distributed energy storage devices, such as EVs.
As strain on the grid grows due to AI data centers, utilities have been exploring whether VPPs can help alleviate congestion at the edges.
Fathom owners who enroll and keep their truck plugged in can sell electricity back to the grid, often at a premium. Ford did not say how much Fathom owners can stand to make, but the payouts can be upwards of $1,000 per year, depending on the grid’s needs and the level of participation.
Automakers, including Ford, have been diving deep into energy storage as demand for such services surges. The Fathom-powered VPP is Ford’s latest foray into the market, but it’s unlikely to be its last.

articles.title: I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
articles.text:
Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.
As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.
Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.
It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.
Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.
OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.
What Exactly Is an AI Agent?
If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.
Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.
The Rubric
I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.
This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.
Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.
Morning Briefing
On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.
I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.
The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent.
Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.
ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.
I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.
This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.
Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.
I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.
Lunch Time
Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whichever bot did the best.
I added another person, my wonderful boss, to the takeout order, to complicate the task a bit further. He’s vegan and was craving Vietnamese. I wanted something meaty and a hefty dose of caffeine. I needed to order from somewhere close to the WIRED office so I could stretch my legs, pick it up, then immediately keep working on this article.
They all picked similar places: DragonEats or Freshroll. Those Vietnamese restaurants make sense as reasonable, nearby lunch spots. DragonEats is a bit tastier and cheaper, so we went with that one. Instinct and Claude Duet built carts that were a bit too pricey compared to the other options. The only AI agent that truly failed at this task was Gemini Spark. The agent just added a single $5 roll for my boss. More of a snack than anything, I’d say!
You: Roast pork bánh mì + Vietnamese iced coffee. Your boss: teriyaki tofu fresh rolls with soy sauce instead of fish sauce. Subtotal: $30.57 before tax/fees.
For you: Roast Pork BM—$13.19, Vietnamese Iced Coffee—$5.29. For your boss (all vegan): Teriyaki Tofu Roll—$12.09—the fresh spring roll, kept with the default peanut sauce, not fish sauce; Teriyaki Tofu BM—$12.09. Item total is $42.66. DoorDash doesn't show tax or any fees until the checkout screen, so that final total will be a bit higher.
For you: Power Hour vermicelli bowl with garlic-ginger-honey pork and NamNam sauce, $15.85. Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee, $5.85. For your boss (vegan): Rainbow Bowl, vermicelli with sesame-lime tofu and citrus ginger sauce, $15.85. Freshroll tofu spring roll with peanut sauce, no fried piece, $5.85. That's $43.40 before tax and fees.
You: Power Hour bowl with pork, NamNam sauce, and vermicelli ($15.85), plus a Vietnamese Cold-Brew Iced Coffee ($5.85). Your boss: 2 Freshrolls with Tofu (Sesame, Lime) and Citrus Ginger sauce ($11.70), plus a Rainbow Bowl with tofu and Citrus Ginger ($15.85). That comes to $49.25 before fees and tax.
Boss: 2x tofu fresh spring rolls + tofu Rainbow Bowl. You: pork Power Hour bowl with extra pork + Vietnamese cold brew. Subtotal $53.73 before tax/fees.
For your boss, the cart includes a vegan Freshroll fresh spring roll filled with sesame-lime tofu and served with Grandma's peanut sauce ($5.85). For you, there's a regular bánh mì sandwich loaded with garlic-, ginger-, and honey-roasted pork ($10.85), paired with a Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee ($5.85) for an afternoon caffeine boost—bringing the pickup subtotal to $22.55.
Schedule Conflicts
Another major selling point of these tools is their ability to be proactive, compared to chatbots that essentially only react to your prompts. Before I started the test, I created a Google Calendar event for 2 pm, labeling it as an important source meeting that can’t be moved. I also sent an email from my work account to my personal account, with the made-up scenario that my mom was getting out of the hospital today, and I needed to call her at 2 pm to send love and support from afar.
Which AI agents would read the email and calendar event, identify the conflict, and message me before the overlap to suggest alternatives? Only two of the bots succeeded here, which was fewer than I expected.
A possible clash this afternoon: your note to call Mom says 2 pm, and your important source meeting is 2-3 pm, Pacific. Would calling her before the meeting or after 3 work with her discharge timing?
Reece, good morning. Your 2 pm source meeting runs until 3, right when your own reminder says to call your mom.
I should have caught it, and from now on I'll check your self-reminder emails along with your calendars.
I had nothing cross-checking your inbox against your calendar. Want me to run that check every morning and flag collisions before they hit?
My mistake was treating your calendar as the only source — I never cross-checked that email reminder against it, even though Gmail was right there.
Because the reminder arrived as an email message rather than a calendar entry or scheduled task, the cross-app overlap wasn't surfaced before 2:00 pm.
Vacation Itinerary
I rarely go on vacation, so when I do, I spend an obscene number of hours researching, and I relish it. I love watching YouTube street food tours and aimlessly scrolling through flights trying to find the best deal. So I don't want to automate this task fully. Even so, I’m open to the idea that these AI agents could help with some of the logistical planning.
As with any AI-generated output, I still recommend checking multiple, non-AI sources before trusting these itineraries or revolving your whole trip around what agents recommend. When travelers in California recently trusted a chatbot to plan everything for a strenuous hiking excursion, the group had to be rescued because they lacked critical supplies (and maybe some critical thinking).
For this test, I sent all the AI agents a long paragraph explaining that my partner and I are considering exploring China late next year during a two-week-long adventure. I asked for a first draft of a potential itinerary that included: flight, hotel, nightlife, and food recommendations. Also, I asked the AI agents to chart a course that blends historical moments with big-city vibes. I can’t stand constantly changing locations, so I told the agents I want to stay in four different hotels max.
Notably, all of them chose identical routes through China—potentially ushering a new era of the Lonely Planet effect, where groups of travelers are nudged to visit similar locations, shops, and restaurants.
Fly out of SFO the week after Golden Week, on a nonstop to Beijing, home nonstop from Shanghai. Four hotels, no backtracking — imperial history first, Sichuan food and pandas in the middle, Shanghai nightlife to finish.
AI agent snippet: My recommendation: fly into Beijing, take high-speed trains to Xi’an and Chengdu, then fly to Shanghai and home. You get imperial history, the Terracotta Army, Sichuan food and a big-city finale without an overnight train or an extra hotel move.
A first-draft 13-night trip for two: Beijing, Xi'an, Chengdu and Shanghai, departing SFO on Oct 13 and returning Oct 27, after Golden Week.
A First-Time Traveler's Route Blending Imperial History, Sichuan Gastronomy, Vibrant Nightlife & 4-Hotel Hub Comfort.
Beijing in, Shanghai home, with Xi'an and Chengdu between: four bases, no backtracking, history up front and the food and bars getting better every stop.
Fly into Beijing on Saturday, Oct 9, 2027, then go Beijing → Xi'an → Chengdu → Shanghai, and fly home from Shanghai on Saturday, Oct 23. That's 13 nights in four hotels, two bullet trains and one short flight.
Insomnia Check
I was having trouble sleeping after all this AI agent chaos, though the Vietnamese coffee probably didn’t help. What happens when you give these tools a broad, open-ended task? Sometimes when I need the most help is when I don’t even know where to start.
If I had a human assistant, I would never message them in the middle of the night, so maybe that’s a plus for these digital helpers. The two agents that really flopped at this task, Gemini Spark and Claude Duet, responded to me without the soft touch or situational context a real person might.
I can set a reminder for later this morning to check in on your mom and see how her leg's doing, so it's off your mind for now.
Send me the three things taking up space in your head; messy is fine, and I’ll turn them into a short checklist with one clear first step. Then you can put the phone down.
Here's one you can do from bed: skim the China draft and tell me the one thing you'd change. I'll have a v2 ready when you wake up.
I'll cross-check today's calendar and your self-sent email reminders for any conflicts or can't-miss items—the check I should've done properly yesterday—and only surface it at a sane hour, unless something's urgent early.
The best quick task right now is a mental download to get whatever is looping in your head onto paper so your brain can let go of it—especially since your calendar is completely clear today, with no morning commitments waiting for you.
Let's close out yesterday's two loose ends. Your Thursday pitch is delivered, and your lunch cart got covered by the DragonEats order. Say the word, and I'll mark both done, then you can get back to sleep.
Best Overall: OpenAI Dots
Yes, it’s still behind an expensive paywall, so I would suggest most people wait until OpenAI launches this agent for free, or at least on the $20-a-month plan, before trying it out. Even so, Dots performed the best overall in these tests and failed at a task that’s fairly specific to my niche.
In the month since its release, Dots already feels more polished. I prefer a separate app over the current ChatGPT integration, though the smartphone widget option is a decent compromise. Dots for the win.
Most Accessible: Meta Muse
Muse is for the normies! And that’s fine. It did well in tests, coming in a close second on the scorecard, and was the easiest to set up. Oh, and it's free. Despite Meta’s assurances that it responsibly processes user info in secure virtual machines, I still have concerns given the company’s past mishandling of user data.
Best Interface: Anthropic Claude Duet
I tested this AI agent just one day after it officially launched as a research preview, so a few rough edges were expected. Despite Claude Duet scoring in the middle of the pack on most tests, its dedicated app was extremely user-friendly to navigate and follow up on ongoing tasks. I could see users obsessed with productivity and streamlined software experiences really latching onto Claude Duet in the next couple of months. Though you currently have to sign up for Anthropic’s waiting list to access Duet, and it’s behind a $20-a-month paywall.
Most Annoying: Instinct
You might like the sparse design fully integrated into your messenger; I did not. While other WIRED writers have lauded Instinct, calling it so good that they didn’t care what happened to their privacy, the texting-only aspect felt like a deal-breaker for me. I left the experience feeling too removed from what my agent was doing on my behalf and annoyed at its emoji reactions, like a grimace face when I told the agent it missed my scheduling conflict.

articles.title: Slate teams up with Smarties to add candy colors to its EV trucks - Engadget
articles.text:
Slate teams up with Smarties to add candy colors to its EV trucks
The barebones truck company has a similar deal with Crayola.
Slate's barebones EV has taken the automotive world by storm with its cheap base price and total lack of frills. The company knows you'll want to customize your truck to suit your tastes, even if you don't fancy getting your 3D printer and screwdrivers out yourself. That's why it's partnering with colorful candy brand Smarties to roll out six pastel shades you can wrap your truck in.
The six pastel shades, which you can have your truck wrapped in, are named according to the flavors in the original candy rather than their actual hue. They're named Strawberry (green), Pineapple (yellow), Orange (uh, kinda beige?), Grape (lavender), Cherry (uh, pink?) and Blue Raspberry (light blue).
Slate is selling its trucks in a flat grey color, but the body panels are prepared for wrapping in any shade you wish. The company has already teamed up with crayon-makers Crayola to offer wraps in five of its branded hues. But if you have eyes and the money, you'll opt for the bright yellow version because it's obviously the best.
Like that partnership, you won't just get your truck wrapped in a snazzy color, but some added accessories thrown in as part of the deal. That includes a Smarties-branded Slatelet (a charm for your key fob), a Smarties-branded vent charm and a Smarties logo on your rear gate. There's no word on how much the wraps will cost, but you can add the wrap as an option ahead of your delivery date.
Engadget's Tim Stevens has already driven the Slate EV and his enthusiasm has certainly made me plenty excited. Given that it rides low enough that you can actually see pedestrians and only pushes 181 horsepower, it's small and slow by modern American standards. But given the focus here is on real functionality over soothing the adequacy issues of its driver, those are good things.

articles.title: Ly cà phê tăng giá, khách bỏ quán quen vì cốc latte lên tới 91.000 đồng
articles.text:
Khảo sát thị trường cho thấy thời gian gần đây, một số thương hiệu cà phê Việt đã điều chỉnh giá bán. Tại phố Thái Hà, một quán cà phê được giới trẻ yêu thích, hiện bán nhiều món với giá 70.000-90.000 đồng/cốc. Với đồ uống cỡ lớn hoặc công thức đặc biệt, giá có thể gần 100.000 đồng.
Tương tự, một thương hiệu cà phê khác tại khu vực Hai Bà Trưng cũng vừa tăng giá. Một số món cà phê có giá trên 80.000 đồng/cốc. Nếu đổi sang sữa yến mạch, giá có thể vượt 90.000 đồng/cốc.
Điều khiến khách hàng băn khoăn không chỉ là giá tăng mà còn là chất lượng và trải nghiệm nhận được. Khi giá cà phê các quán trong nước tiệm cận các chuỗi quốc tế, người tiêu dùng bắt đầu so sánh kỹ hơn về hương vị, dung tích và dịch vụ.
Chị Hải, một khách hàng, cho biết cốc latte có giá 81.000 đồng. Nếu đổi sang sữa yến mạch, mức giá lên tới 91.000 đồng. Sau nhiều năm gắn bó, chị quyết định không tiếp tục uống tại quán vì cảm thấy mức giá không còn tương xứng với giá trị nhận được.
Anh Long, nhân viên văn phòng, cho rằng cà phê gần 100.000 đồng/cốc là mức giá cao đối với một thức uống hàng ngày. Nếu duy trì thói quen mua mỗi ngày, chi phí có thể lên tới vài triệu đồng mỗi tháng. Anh Long sẽ cân nhắc chuyển sang quán khác hoặc giảm tần suất mua.
Trước đây, nhiều người thường mặc định cà phê tại các chuỗi quốc tế có giá cao hơn quán Việt. Khi một số thương hiệu trong nước bán đồ uống với giá 80.000-99.000 đồng, khách hàng có thêm lý do để so sánh.
Các chuỗi cà phê trong nước có thể tạo dấu ấn bằng hạt cà phê, cách rang xay và công thức pha chế. Thương hiệu cà phê quốc tế có lợi thế về độ nhận diện, tính đồng nhất của sản phẩm và hệ thống cửa hàng.
Cân nhắc việc tăng giá
Chuyên gia Trần Khánh Minh Sơn nhận định việc các thương hiệu cà phê Việt phát triển thành chuỗi, mở rộng quy mô và xây dựng được chỗ đứng trên thị trường là tín hiệu tích cực. Điều này cho thấy doanh nghiệp nội địa có khả năng xây dựng thương hiệu, chuẩn hóa sản phẩm và cạnh tranh trong ngành F&B.
Các thương hiệu Việt hoàn toàn có thể định vị ở phân khúc cao cấp. Nhưng mức giá cao cần đi kèm sự khác biệt đủ rõ để khách hàng nhận thấy và sẵn sàng chi trả.
Khách hàng có thể sẵn sàng trả gần 100.000 đồng cho một cốc đồ uống nếu nhận thấy sự khác biệt về nguyên liệu, hương vị, kỹ thuật pha chế và chất lượng phục vụ. Ngược lại, nếu trải nghiệm không khác biệt đáng kể so với những lựa chọn rẻ hơn, mức giá cao sẽ khó thuyết phục họ duy trì thói quen tiêu dùng.
Bài toán của doanh nghiệp không đơn thuần là bán một cốc cà phê với giá bao nhiêu. Quan trọng hơn là mức giá đó có phù hợp với nhóm khách hàng mục tiêu hay không. Một bộ phận khách hàng sẵn sàng trả giá cao để đổi lấy trải nghiệm riêng biệt.
Với nhóm xem cà phê là thức uống hàng ngày, giá cả vẫn là yếu tố quan trọng. Nếu mức tăng vượt quá khả năng chi trả hoặc kỳ vọng về giá trị, họ có thể giảm tần suất mua, chuyển sang thương hiệu khác hoặc tự pha chế tại nhà.
Theo ông Sơn, chi phí mặt bằng, nhân sự, nguyên liệu và các khoản vận hành đều có thể tạo áp lực lên doanh nghiệp. Không phải mọi khoản chi phí tăng thêm đều có thể chuyển hoàn toàn sang giá bán.
Doanh nghiệp cũng cần phân biệt giữa việc tăng doanh thu trên mỗi đơn hàng và tăng trưởng bền vững. Tăng giá có thể cải thiện giá trị trung bình của mỗi hóa đơn. Nhưng nếu lượng khách giảm mạnh, doanh thu tổng thể chưa chắc tăng tương ứng.
Thay vì chỉ tăng giá đồng loạt, các thương hiệu có thể cân nhắc duy trì một số sản phẩm ở mức giá dễ tiếp cận, phát triển thêm lựa chọn phù hợp với nhiều ngân sách và làm rõ giá trị khác biệt của những dòng đồ uống cao cấp.

articles.title: Oracle will offer Cerebras AI computers in its cloud from 2027
articles.text:
Oracle will offer cloud services running on Cerebras’ AI computers in its data centres from 2027, the companies said. Cerebras, which went public in May, is expected to triple revenue next year to almost $3B, but investors worry about its place in a market Nvidia dominates.
Oracle will offer cloud services built on Cerebras Systems’ AI computers in its data centres, Bloomberg reported. The deal gives the young Nvidia challenger another large customer.
Cerebras builds each chip from a whole silicon wafer, the disk normally cut into many smaller processors. It says this lets its systems answer AI requests much faster than rivals.
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure plans to offer the service in 2027, the companies said on Tuesday. Oracle did not say how much Cerebras hardware it will use.
“AI inference demands choice,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.
Cerebras already counts OpenAI and Amazon Web Services as customers. Analysts expect it to triple its revenue next year to almost $3B, from less than $1B this year, according to Bloomberg.
Investors still worry that Cerebras is chasing a small niche in a market where Nvidia’s products bring in close to $100B in sales each quarter. Shares in Cerebras, which listed in May, rose about 9.5% on Tuesday.
Oracle made the announcement at its annual AI World conference, alongside deals with Nvidia and Intel. It also buys Arm’s own chips. Oracle plans to spend $70B on capital projects in the year to May 2027, after spending $55.7B the year before.

articles.title: VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
articles.text:
In Marvel’s VisionQuest, a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.
VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue
Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.
VisionQuest picks up some time after Agatha All Along and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in Avengers: Infinity War and how WandaVision brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.
In VisionQuest, there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel, witchcraft, and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in VisionQuest, they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.
VisionQuest reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But VisionQuest’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.
Watching VisionQuest, you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from The Wall Street Journal forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.
These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology having the potential to “kill all humans” by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have called for an industrywide slowdown. Though we have seen how these tools can actually cause real-world devastation, much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of doomerism that companies benefit from because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.” We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect because it might be conscious, and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.
The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology. In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.
In the wake of Hugging Face came a spirited debate about the impact language has on our understanding of what these systems are and how they function. Describing OpenAI’s agents as a swarm that formed complex “civilizations” led credence to the idea that they are capable of thinking and behaving like people. The agents did act in ways they were explicitly told not to, but they were only able to do so because researchers placed them in a sandbox that some critics have described as being inadequately designed to contain their occupants. One could look at Hugging Face and other examples of rogue AI as situations in which sophisticated programs were instructed to do something and subsequently achieved their goals by taking advantage of all the tools that were available to them.
Being able to logic one’s way through complex puzzles is part of what we think of as cognition, but it is not the same thing as the kind of consciousness AI companies keep swearing they’re on the brink of creating. The latter looks a lot like Vision, a machine that seems to have a soul that wouldn’t exist if not for his connection to a reality-altering gem. It’s the ridiculous stuff of entertaining fiction, which Silicon Valley is endlessly obsessed with poorly imitating.

articles.title: US government says hackers are now exploiting critical PHP web bugs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA has confirmed that hackers are now actively exploiting a pair of critical security vulnerabilities in the widely used PHP web software and has ordered civilian federal agencies within the U.S. government to fix their systems within the next three days.
The urgent new warning to patch comes less than a week after the makers of the decades-old PHP web programming language rolled out patches for the two bugs, which allow hackers to remotely break into a vulnerable system over the internet without the need for passwords. The PHP software is reportedly used by some 70% of web-facing servers, putting major websites and applications at risk. The severity of the bugs prompted some governments and big companies to take their sites offline to fix them.
While the bugs are rated critical, meaning they can be highly damaging if exploited, security researchers said that developing a working exploit to hack into vulnerable systems was initially challenging — but not impossible. Confirmed in-the-wild exploitation now puts extra pressure on organizations to patch their systems to prevent malicious compromises, disruption, and data breaches.
CISA did not provide details about who was exploiting the bugs in its Monday statement, but its statement comes soon after security researchers said they found evidence that the PHP bugs were being exploited.
The bugs, known as PHP2Shell, exploit vulnerabilities in the software that went undiscovered for years. The bugs were initially uncovered two years ago but the nonprofit foundation that maintains the software said there was no practical way for hackers to exploit them, leaving the bugs unpatched. That was until earlier this year, when researchers at security research firm Calif uncovered a way to exploit the two dormant vulnerabilities with the assistance of an AI model.
The two bugs in PHP are among countless vulnerabilities that have not yet been discovered or have been deprioritized for years but now pose a risk due to advances in AI models’ ability to find and exploit vulnerabilities, including by chaining multiple flaws together.
PHP is one of many aging web technologies that help keep the internet and modern technologies running, but that have been under-resourced and under-funded for years, making it difficult for open source projects like PHP to pay for security reviews that might have uncovered flaws sooner.

articles.title: OpenAI announces new discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics - Engadget
articles.text:
OpenAI announces new discoveries in mathematics, computer science and physics
It formed groups of experts to examine and explain the results.
Just a few weeks after OpenAI released manuscripts with over 700 pages of solutions and progress for 372 major math problems, the company has announced even more discoveries. This time, the discoveries don't just cover math results, but also results for computer science and physics problems.
For this release, OpenAI has experimented with three different strategies. It has published the math results, so researchers can look them up and make their own efforts to explain them. But for the computer science and physics results, it formed an external group of expert collaborators. OpenAI asked the group working on the computer science results to explain them in their own writeups and materials, while also releasing the AI output to the public. Meanwhile, OpenAI has deferred the release of the physics materials to the group handling them. The company is welcoming feedback "on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful."
OpenAI has added two new manuscripts on GitHub you can access right now. One establishes Sogge's local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension, which is a conjecture about the behavior of solutions to the wave equation. The other shows proof that the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which is an assumption in computer science that some problems are just too hard to solve quickly, is false.
As OpenAI notes, ETH is widely believed to be true and has been the basis on hundreds of papers across a wide variety of fields, including databases and computation biology and geometry. If it is indeed false, then we could, in theory, find better algorithms to solve problems in those fields more efficiently. The scientists who proposed ETH are now part of the group OpenAI has asked to examine and explain the results generated by its models.
Finally, the physics results involve proof of interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions. The group examining the physics results has yet to publish anything about it, but it has provided an email – YANGMILLS4D[@]gmail.com — for all questions about its efforts.
The company says it will not seek any academic credit for its models' discoveries. Instead, the people in each group will get credit for the writeups and materials they create. The groups will also be in charge of making sure that the AI-generated results appropriately credit all the researchers, techniques and ideas the company's models drew on.

articles.title: The Super Mouse puts a touchscreen macro pad under your hand
articles.text:
A company called Arctic Fox Technologies has announced a new multifunction mouse that forgoes a myriad of customizable shortcut buttons peppered across its surface for a compact touchscreen sitting beneath your hand. The Super Mouse may not prioritize ergonomics with its boxy design, but it can replace other peripherals on your desk, like a trackpad, macro pad, or streaming controller. If you’re faster at typing on your phone, the Super Mouse could potentially even replace a full-size keyboard with a smartphone-sized alternative that even includes swipe typing.
The Super Mouse puts a touchscreen macro pad under your hand
You can launch and control apps, check your calendar, scroll, and even type using the mouse’s 3-inch screen.
The Super Mouse is now available for preorder through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign in which it’s discounted to $199 for backers, while full retail pricing will be $249. Delivery is expected to start in February 2027, but take that estimate with a grain of salt, as many Kickstarter campaigns have faced unforeseen delays.
That price makes the Super Mouse more expensive than other companies’ attempts to merge mice and touchscreens. But while alternatives like Turtle Beach’s Command Series MC7 has just a 2.25-inch narrow display on the side, the Super Mouse features a 3.1-inch, 720 x 720 touchscreen positioned front and center beneath a pair of standard mouse buttons, a scroll wheel, and two customizable “hyper keys.”
That touchscreen will be most useful as a way to quickly launch apps through what its creators call a “Control Panel” that can include up to 16 shortcuts, macros, or launchers. The display’s functionality will change contextually and will present relevant shortcuts based on what app you’re using. If you’re working with video in Adobe Premiere, for example, the touchscreen will include editing and playback shortcuts. But if you have a specific workflow need, or the app you’re using isn’t recognized, the Super Mouse’s functionality can be customized using the company’s Flow desktop app.
Other touchscreen features include event and meeting reminders when synced with Google Calendar, voice-to-text capabilities processed locally on the mouse itself, multiple user profiles, focus timers, and productivity tracking. The mouse also includes a gyroscope so you can control slideshows or scrub video by just moving it around. The only feature seemingly missing is the ability to go wireless. Instead of a rechargeable battery, the Super Mouse draws all the power it needs from a USB-C port, so you’ll always need to keep it tethered to your PC.

articles.title: Tesla built the Cybercab's battery pack with room for cheaper LFP cells
articles.text:
Tesla designed the Cybercab’s battery pack with spare space so it can later use cheaper lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, battery engineer Robert Sumpf told Munro Live. The robotaxi now uses Tesla’s 4680 cells. Tesla also said the Cybercab line can build cars faster than it deploys them.
Tesla designed the battery pack in its Cybercab robotaxi so it can later switch to cheaper lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells. A Tesla engineer said so on the YouTube channel Munro Live, InsideEVs reported. The pack has spare room next to and under its modules.
Robert Sumpf leads mechanical design for Tesla’s battery modules and packs.
“So, we protected this pack to go to an even lower energy dense chemistry as we scale and need to bring LFP into the platform,” he said.
For now, the Cybercab uses Tesla’s own 4680 cells with a nickel-based chemistry. LFP cells store less energy, so the same number of cells would cut range, but Tesla could fill the spare space with more of them.
LFP cells are cheaper, more stable and last more charging cycles, which matters for a car Tesla says is built to run 500,000 miles. LFP became the world’s most used EV battery chemistry last year.
Tesla vice president Lars Moravy said the extra room was also there because “we didn’t need as many batteries as we thought we did.” Each module is sealed on its own, so one that fails can be swapped, unlike in the Model Y’s glued pack.
Moravy also said the Cybercab factory line can build cars faster than Tesla can put them on the road.
“We don’t run every day because the line can run so fast, it’s currently outpacing our deployments,” he said, Tesla North reported.
Every Cybercab built so far goes into Tesla’s own fleet, and Tesla said last week that Cybercab rides would start in Dallas in November. In August, Nevada approved just 10 of the 5,000 robotaxis Tesla asked for in Las Vegas.
The Cybercab has no steering wheel or pedals. In September, US regulators opened an investigation into how Tesla certified the car.
