articles.title: Apple unveils new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 chip | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple on Tuesday unveiled its new 14-inch MacBook Pro, powered by its latest M6 chip. The new MacBook Pro has 24 hours of battery life and now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity. The laptop starts at $1,999 and is available in space black and silver.
Apple also announced its latest iMac, which is also powered by the M6 chip. The tech giant revealed the new devices just a day before its “Pro and Tell” event scheduled for Wednesday. On Monday, Apple announced its new iPad mini.
The tech giant says the M6 chip features a 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core and a 12-core GPU that delivers more responsive performance, up to 30% faster graphics, and up to 25% faster AI workloads compared with the M5 chip.
The M6 delivers up to 13 times the LLM prompt-processing speed of the M1 MacBook Pro and up to 1.3 times faster performance than the M5 model, Apple says.
The M6 MacBook Pro starts with 16GB of unified memory, configurable up to 32GB, and has memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s, up from the 153GB/s on the M5 chip.
It includes HDMI, MagSafe 3, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an SDXC card slot, and a headphone jack. Like previous models, the laptop features a 12-megapixel camera.
The M6 MacBook Pro supports fast charging, reaching up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with a compatible high-wattage USB-C power adapter.
As for the new M6-powered iMac, it features a faster CPU and GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every core. Apple says the M6 delivers smooth multitasking and powerful performance for everyday apps, photo editing, and video production.
The new iMac starts at $1,499 and comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver.
The company also notes that the new iMac delivers up to five times faster on-device AI performance than the M4 model. It features a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, an advanced camera and audio system, up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports, color-matched accessories, and macOS 27.
Both the new MacBook Pro and iMac can be preordered starting October 28 and will be available starting November 6.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 27/10: Thế giới giảm, trong nước chờ điều chỉnh
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong phiên giao dịch đầu tuần (26/10) quay đầu giảm sau khi tăng mạnh vào phiên cuối tuần trước.
Chốt phiên giao dịch 26/10, theo Reuters, giá dầu Brent giảm 0,78%, xuống còn 115,8 USD/thùng. Còn giá dầu WTI của Mỹ hạ 1,46%, về mức 101,76 USD/thùng.
Đầu phiên giao dịch hôm nay (27/10), giá dầu WTI tiếp tục đi xuống.
Theo dữ liệu từ Oilprice, vào lúc 6h27' ngày 27/10 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent vẫn được niêm yết ở mức 115,8 USD/thùng. Trong khi giá dầu WTI được điều chỉnh xuống mức 101,4 USD/thùng, giảm 0,37% so với phiên liền trước.
Giá dầu thế giới đảo chiều đi xuống sau khi chạm mức cao nhất gần 6 tháng, trong bối cảnh kỳ vọng căng thẳng Mỹ - Iran hạ nhiệt, dù nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung tại Trung Đông vẫn hiện hữu.
Kỳ vọng về một bước đột phá trong ngoại giao nhằm giải quyết xung đột tại Trung Đông đã gây sức ép lên giá dầu.
Theo một số nguồn tin, các nhà trung gian hòa giải của Qatar đã tới Tehran vào ngày 25/10, nhằm phối hợp với Mỹ tìm cách hạ nhiệt căng thẳng trong khu vực.
Ngày 26/10, Saudi Arabia, Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ và Pakistan (những nước thuộc Hiệp ước Mecca) đã tiến hành các cuộc hội đàm với quan chức Iran tại Tehran nhằm ngăn chặn nguy cơ leo thang xung đột. Đây là cuộc tiếp xúc cấp cao đầu tiên giữa các bên kể từ khi những cuộc tấn công của lực lượng Houthi do Iran hậu thuẫn nhằm vào Saudi Arabia trở thành một điểm nóng trong cuộc xung đột.
Truyền thông nhà nước Iran đưa tin, sau cuộc gặp này, 4 nước đã nhất trí tiếp tục đối thoại nhằm tăng cường hợp tác về hòa bình và an ninh.
Bên cạnh đó, lo ngại gián đoạn nguồn cung năng lượng từ Trung Đông tiếp tục gây sức ép lên thị trường sau các cuộc tấn công của lực lượng Houthi nhằm vào Saudi Arabia.
Lực lượng Houthi ở Yemen vào cuối tuần qua tuyên bố đã tấn công các trạm bơm trên đường ống dẫn dầu thô Đông - Tây của Saudi Arabia và sân bay Riyadh.
Trong khi đó, liên minh quân sự do Saudi Arabia dẫn đầu tại Yemen cho biết đã bắn hạ 3 máy bay không người lái nhằm vào thủ đô Riyadh và các khu vực phía nam của nước này trong ngày 26/10.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Theo kế hoạch, liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính sẽ tiến hành điều chỉnh giá xăng dầu trong nước vào chiều thứ Năm (ngày 29/10).
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (27/10) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 22/10, giá xăng E5RON92 giảm 1.610 đồng/lít so với kỳ trước, giá bán lẻ không cao hơn 25.361 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá xăng E10RON95-III hạ 1.816 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 25.213 đồng/lít.
Trong khi đó, giá dầu diesel 0.05S được điều chỉnh tăng 444 đồng/lít, lên mức tối đa 29.550 đồng/lít.
Còn giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S được điều chỉnh tăng 1.238 đồng/kg, giá bán không cao hơn 23.373 đồng/kg.
Dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương cho thấy, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: Apple launches 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 and 24-hour battery
articles.text:
Apple has updated its 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip, promising faster graphics, better on-device AI performance, and up to 24 hours of battery life, the longest runtime the company has offered in a Mac.
The new MacBook Pro was announced today alongside a refreshed iMac. Pre-orders open on Wednesday in 35 countries, with deliveries and in-store availability starting on November 6.
The laptop looks much the same as its predecessor, and it comes in space black and silver and retains three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, an SD card slot, a headphone jack, and MagSafe charging.
The main change is happening inside. The M6 has 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, two more of each than the M5 in last year’s model.
Every GPU core also includes a Neural Accelerator designed to speed up AI workloads. Apple claims the M6 has the fastest CPU core in the world, based on its own tests.
Compared with the M5 MacBook Pro, Apple says the new model delivers up to 30% faster graphics performance and runs AI tasks, such as processing a large language model locally, up to 25% faster.
The Neural Engine, which handles tasks such as image generation and photo enhancement, is up to 1.9 times faster.
Apple also points to improvements in everyday creative and development work. Rendering a 3D scene in Blender and building an app in Xcode are both up to 1.3 times faster, according to the company. All these figures come from Apple’s own testing.
The gains are more pronounced for people upgrading from older machines. Compared with the 13-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 chip from 2020, Apple claims up to 11 times faster graphics and 13 times faster AI performance.
Battery life reaches up to 24 hours, which Apple says is a record for the Mac. Performance remains the same whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. With a higher-wattage power adapter, it can charge to 50% in around 30 minutes.
The Liquid Retina XDR display remains unchanged, offering up to 1,600 nits of brightness for HDR content. Buyers can opt for a nano-texture finish to reduce glare. The new model also supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 and can drive two external displays. Memory starts at 16GB and can be configured up to 32GB.
“With the powerful M6 chip, we’re taking performance to the next level,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of hardware engineering.
The MacBook Pro ships with macOS 27, which introduces Apple’s new AI-powered Siri to the Mac. The assistant can search messages, emails, and photos, as well as perform actions across apps.
It remains in beta, supports six languages, and has daily usage limits. Apple first introduced the assistant on the iPhone with iOS 27.2.
The new MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 in the US and £1,999 in the UK. That matches the M5 model’s price immediately before launch, but not its original price.
Apple raised the starting price by $400 in June, from $1,599, as memory and storage costs increased, EveryMac reported.
Apple also highlighted the materials used in the laptop: the enclosure is made from 100% recycled aluminium, while the battery uses 100% recycled cobalt.

articles.title: Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
articles.text:
Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market.
Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
Anthropic’s planned IPO raises questions over whether it can maintain its safe and responsible AI priorities.
Sam Altman, the CEO of Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, has cited investor pressures as one reason the company is not pursuing an IPO this year. Anthropic hopes it can resist investor pressures with a mind-boggling governance structure.
A “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before…creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.”
University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told The Verge that Anthropic has proposed going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested. But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market.
Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities. Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively.
Another key safeguard aims to protect Anthropic’s mission by limiting shareholder influence over one of the biggest levers of corporate power: the company’s board of directors. Directors oversee the company and appoint its leadership, including the CEO. Directors can also hold executive roles, as is the case with Anthropic, with CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei both sitting on the board.
Shareholders typically have considerable sway over who sits on the board, giving them a means to replace directors or push for changes if they are unhappy with how the company is being run. For example, if shareholders are unhappy at what they perceive as unnecessary delays to market for optional safety testing, they may remove directors and replace them with ones more aligned with their interests, such as making money and being less cautious.
“Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.”
Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all. Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.
The trust is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first.
Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats. However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters. Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote. This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told The Verge.
The prospectus says Founder LLC will “initially” be seven of Anthropic’s founders: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah. “Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members.” Notably absent is another cofounder, Ben Mann, who co-leads the company’s experimental Anthropic Labs arm, as reported by The San Francisco Standard.
All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told The Verge. “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.”
Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling The Verge that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions.
“Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well. But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”
And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures. Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns. Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety.
Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving. In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders. Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety.
Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it. Once that happens, ordinary shareholders could gain the power to weaken the trust’s protections, even against the wishes of the trustees, and without the support of the founders or employees, who hold different classes of stock, Dammann told The Verge. Other means of subverting the trust also exist, he explained, including coordinated action by the public shareholders, employee stockholders, and founders.
For now, it seems, Anthropic can probably have it both ways. But the protections designed to preserve its commitment to AI safety are far from ironclad, and much depends on market pressures, whether its founders stick around, and directions of the trust. Dammann said he sees a “fundamental dilemma that cannot be resolved in a fully satisfactory way” between Anthropic’s mission and investor demands. As long as things are going well, this tension may be manageable. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well,” Dammann said. “But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”

articles.title: Apple rolls out iOS 27.2 with new Siri AI languages and security fixes | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Apple has rolled out its latest iOS 27.2 update for iPhones and iPads, featuring expanded language support and improved memory functions for Siri AI, suggestions in messages, and Apple Pencil support for the foldable iPhone Duo.
With the new software update, Siri AI can now be used in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, in beta. Apple says the AI assistant can now remember details from past conversations and answer accordingly. The ability for AI assistants to remember a person’s preferences have been a key area of focus for AI model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, whose assistants now do a better job at recalling facts and choices related to users.
Apart from its own suggestions and answers, Siri can also tap into sources like photos attached in Messages, calendar event attendees, voicemails, Safari history, and reading lists. Users can define what apps they might want to exclude from Siri AI’s memories.
While the iPhone Duo is facing some display-related problems for early buyers, Apple is adding more features with the update. iOS 27.2 brings Apple Pencil support for the foldable in apps like Notes and Preview. What’s more, users can use the Edge Light effect to highlight their face better during video calls.
The new software version also adds features for FaceTime, including streaming via front and rear camera simultaneously through Dual Capture for group call, and the ability to add a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call.
Users on iOS 27.2 will get suggestions to add a message as an item in a reminder or an event in a calendar. Plus, users can edit captions or add comments in Shared Albums along with reminders of the expiry date of the folder.
The update also refreshes the Podcast app, which will show new episodes from the shows you follow and also the episodes that you are currently listening to.
Apple has also added Multiview to iPhone so viewers can watch up to four live sport streams simultaneously on Apple TV such as Major League Soccer (MLS), Formula 1 (F1) in the U.S., and Friday Night Baseball doubleheaders during the Major League Baseball (MLB) season. Users can also view multiple feeds of F1 during the broadcast.
iOS 27.2 also packs in over 160 security fixes, according to the company’s release documentation. Many of the bug fixes were also backported so that users running the older iOS 26 software can benefit from the fixes.
Apple says that about 80% of iPhone owners are still running iOS 26.
Meanwhile, Apple backported a specific bug fix to users of iOS 18, first released in 2024, which Apple says may have been exploited “in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.” This is standard language that Apple uses when someone’s phone has been compromised by government spyware or a law enforcement forensic device, but did not provide specifics about who was exploiting it.

articles.title: AI disinformation is outpacing platform moderation before US midterms
articles.text:
AI-generated election misinformation is spreading across social media ahead of the US midterm elections, and experts warn that much of it may be escaping detection as platforms scale back human moderation and rely more heavily on automated systems.
AI tools make it cheap to produce convincing fake images, videos, and claims in large volumes. Meanwhile, major social networks have reduced some of the teams responsible for checking content, leaving automated filters and users to catch more of the falsehoods.
“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” Frances Haugen, the former Facebook data engineer who became a whistleblower, told The Guardian.
Haugen also explained how people spreading misinformation can evade moderation. By making small changes to each version of a false claim, they can produce posts that get past automated filters even when similar content has already been flagged.
A rumour involving Texas Senate candidate James Talarico shows how quickly such claims can spread.
Earlier this month, posts on X claimed that the Democratic candidate was receiving treatment at a mental health centre in Ohio, when in reality, he was at home with the flu.
The hospital and Talarico denied the claim within hours, La Voce di New York reported. But the rumour continued circulating for days.
Researchers at the Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas, which monitors misinformation targeting Latino voters, found that the story changed as it spread through Spanish-language media.
It evolved into a false claim that Talarico had attempted to take his own life. Correcting the original allegation did not stop the altered version from circulating, researchers said.
Roberta Braga, the institute’s founder, said platforms apply their rules less consistently to Spanish-language content than to English-language posts.
“Now that they’re using AI to do a lot of the content moderation, even more is likely slipping through the cracks,” she said.
AI-generated content is also appearing in official campaign advertising. Ken Paxton, the Republican challenging Talarico, ran an advertisement featuring AI-generated images of the Democratic candidate.
The ad disclosed its use of AI, and some states have introduced rules requiring such disclosures, including Pennsylvania.
The major platforms have different approaches to political misinformation, but their rules cover only certain types of content. Meta labels AI-generated images it can identify and requires political advertisers to disclose AI use.
YouTube prohibits false claims about when, where, and how people can vote. X relies largely on its crowdsourced Community Notes system.
Many other misleading political claims fall outside these specific rules.
Meta and X did not respond to The Guardian’s requests for comment. YouTube said the same guidelines apply to all users, including political candidates.
The issue extends beyond the US. In Spain, a political party is facing a court complaint over a deepfake election video.
As election campaigns increasingly use AI to create and distribute content, the challenge for platforms is not simply identifying synthetic media. It is also catching false claims that change as they spread, across languages and communities, faster than corrections can follow.

articles.title: Meta’s $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water
articles.text:
When attorneys general from across the US announced a $17 billion settlement with Meta this summer, the sum was unprecedented. But a ruling last week by a New Mexico judge blew that number out of the water. The judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to resolve claims that Meta misled users around the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and related incidents. Similar claims were resolved by the settlement with most other states. The outcome raised an obvious question: Should these states have asked for more?
Meta’s $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water
Should states have sought more in their kids online safety settlement?
The answer depends on a mix of factors, including whether the $25 billion order stands up to Meta’s legal challenges. Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement that the company is “confident we will prevail on appeal” and called New Mexico’s lawsuit an attempt to impose “a tax on speech.” If the fine sticks, however, it could create a new appetite for Big Tech’s opponents to stick it out in court — or ask for bigger payouts to settle.
“For the settling AGs, they’re going to look at this and maybe experience some regret for all the claims that they waived, and start looking around and trying to figure out what’s left that they didn’t waive, if they can try to get some money like this too,” says Daphne Keller, director of platform regulation at the Stanford Program in Law, Science & Technology. For the many individuals, school districts, and tribes with outstanding claims, “this is very encouraging and will make them hopeful that continuing to litigate aggressively will lead to a big payout,” Keller says.
The $25 billion court order covered millions of violations of New Mexico’s unfair practices law, after a jury found Meta had misled users about how it protected their data and policed misinformation and hate speech – claims stemming from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal. In most states, such claims were covered by a section of the kids online safety settlement, resolved with a $459 million payment.
While that number looks comparatively puny, there were upsides to taking it. A settlement provided more certainty and an expedited payout for states even though Meta will be making the payments over 10 years. It also secured product commitments from Meta, like restrictions on teen usage, that might have been more difficult to get from a court ruling. And it allowed those to be implemented soon after the settlement was approved, which advocates say is important to prevent further harm to kids. Other state attorneys general also may have been working with different laws or evidence that could result in outcomes different from those obtained in New Mexico.
“Assuming that even a fraction of this award gets upheld, then they clearly took pennies on the dollar compared to New Mexico”
But New Mexico’s win, combined with other recent legal victories for AGs and private plaintiffs — including a separate judgment of nearly $1 billion against Meta in New Mexico — may embolden anyone still litigating privacy and kids online safety cases. “Assuming that even a fraction of this award gets upheld, then they clearly took pennies on the dollar compared to New Mexico,” Keller says of the settling states. Imagining she’s an AG with similar claims — like public false statements about privacy or content moderation — “I become less willing to settle in those cases,” Keller adds. “Or if I do settle, I ask for more.”
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose state avoided joining the Meta settlement, seemed to take the latest New Mexico ruling as a validation. “As I said at the time, the multi-state settlement with Meta was a slap on the wrist,” Utheimer wrote on X. “Florida isn’t going to sell out to Meta. We’re going to hold them accountable.” The District of Columbia could be the next place to test whether New Mexico’s win can be replicated since it did not settle its Cambridge Analytica claims and has continued pursuing its lawsuit in court.
“Any one, or 10, or 50 of them could hit the jackpot”
While the AGs who joined the settlement can’t pursue covered claims against Meta anymore, they could still push for more in cases against other social media defendants, including TikTok, YouTube, and Snap. And those who weren’t part of the Meta settlement, including school districts and individuals, may be encouraged to continue pushing ahead. “Realistically, there’s so many cases, it’s not feasible that every single case can have an outcome like this,” says Keller. “Meta actually would go broke because the multipliers are so large. But any one, or 10, or 50 of them could hit the jackpot.”
States have stepped in to pursue tech policy and competition cases where the federal government has declined to, but the wide range of potential outcomes for each state presents its own challenges. As Congress has stalled on major tech policy bills and the Trump administration has often favored lighter regulation on tech, Colorado Law associate professor Blake Reid sees recent cases as a “move toward state-level tech policy.”
“The trick of that is, now you have 50 states that all have different sets of resources, and different sets of politics, and different sets of incentives, and frankly just different skill levels in terms of the sophistication that it takes to do litigation at this scale,” Reid says. “And it’s the same Meta, but now it’s up to 50 small opponents that are going to break in different ways.”
As for whether the $25 billion ruling makes other states rethink their strategy, Reid says there could be a range of approaches, depending partly on whether the figure is upheld on appeal and whether Meta loses yet more cases. “Is that a game that every state attorney general wants to play?” he asks. “And I think the settlement in the other case suggests maybe not.” Still, the new figure may change what AGs think they can achieve in court. And the more losses Meta and other tech companies rack up, the more ambitious they might get.

articles.title: Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Japanese internet company GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders.
The IT and internet services giant said on its blog that it believes the attacker has published information allegedly linked to customers and its business. However, the contents are still being verified and the full extent of the incident remains unclear.
GMO Internet has since advised customers to reset their passwords, amid receiving reports of “unauthorized operations” performed on customer trading accounts. The company said 27,000 servers may be affected by the breach.
A spokesperson for GMO Internet did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.
The incident comes about a week after the Japanese firm’s cybersecurity unit separately reported finding evidence that a Chinese AI-enabled penetration testing tool called Artex had been used in hacks targeting companies across Japan. However, the company said it has not publicly established a connection between Artex and the breach of Onamae.
The Artex tool was also used to hack financial institutions in South Korea in September, according to a report by CrowdStrike earlier this month. The attacks largely relied on exploiting weak security controls, such as a lack of multi-factor authentication. Artex’s Chinese developer has since stopped public updates and made the AI security tool closed-source after it was linked to cyberattacks targeting banks, per Reuters.
A spokesperson at Japan’s Financial Service Agency (FSA) told TechCrunch that it issued guidance in May urging financial institutions to prepare for a rise in cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The regulator called for stronger basic defenses, including “vulnerability management, defense-in-depth and incident preparedness,” while encouraging firms to use AI and other security tools, the spokesperson added.
Here’s the timeline of the Onamae breach.
October 21: GMO Internet shut down its Onamae Desktop Cloud service after discovering unauthorized access had occurred to its systems without permission. The IT firm also received an email from hackers demanding about 8 billion yen (~$50 million).
October 22: The Japanese company reported the incident to Japanese police and shared another public update.
October 24: GMO Internet said it would offer customers compensation and alternative service while seeking help from government agencies.
October 25-26: The company began collecting devices from customers to detect malware and better understand the damage.
October 27: The Japanese IT firm said a suspected attacker had posted information that appeared to be linked to the company and its customers. GMO said it was still checking whether the information was genuine.

articles.title: Intel to buy quantum software firm Classiq for about $2.3bn
articles.text:
Intel has agreed to buy Classiq, an Israeli startup that makes software for programming quantum computers.
The chipmaker announced the deal on Monday without giving a price, but it is worth about $2.3bn, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Intel declined to comment on the figure.
Quantum computers use qubits, which can handle certain problems, such as simulating molecules, far faster than ordinary chips. But writing programs for them is hard and usually needs specialists.
Classiq tries to make that easier. Its platform lets developers describe what they want a program to do and then designs the quantum circuit for them, much as chip design software does for regular processors. It works across different types of quantum hardware, and customers include BMW and HSBC.
Intel has worked on quantum computing since 2015, building qubits on silicon with the same equipment it uses for ordinary chips.
Adding Classiq would give it what the industry calls a full stack: both the processors and the software to use them.
“Joining forces with Classiq transforms Intel’s Quantum Computing Group into a full-stack quantum computing business,” said Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan.
Intel said it would keep Classiq’s software working with other companies’ quantum hardware, and that Classiq would become its global development centre for quantum computing. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval.
Classiq was founded by chief executive Nir Minerbi, Amir Naveh and Yehuda Naveh. It has raised just over $200m and was valued at about $600m to $700m in 2025, Israeli outlet Calcalist reported, according to Ynet.
Tan was among Classiq’s investors, joining its 2022 and 2025 funding rounds. He did not take part in the deal talks because of that stake, Calcalist reported. Tan’s links to companies that do business with Intel have drawn attention before.
The purchase comes as Intel’s turnaround gathers pace. Its shares have nearly tripled this year, and in August it sold $15bn of stock to fund its chip factories.

articles.title: Billionaire Palmer Luckey isn't leaving California over the wealth tax | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Palmer Luckey has been a California billionaire since he was 21 years old, when he sold his first company, virtual reality headset maker Oculus VR, to Facebook for $2 billion in 2014. His current company, defense tech firm Anduril, is headquartered in Costa Mesa, California, not far from Long Beach, where Luckey grew up. And Anduril is worth far more. It was last valued at $61 billion.
While Luckey clearly despises the proposed California billionaire wealth tax, a ballot measure that would tax the net worth of the state’s richest residents, he said he’s not leaving California over it.
“I think that this tax act, if you can call it a tax, is going to cause a lot of problems. It’s causing a lot of people to run who I don’t want to be running. It’s going to cause companies that I work with to leave the state, which is a problem for me. As of right now, though, I’m not running. I am staying. I think California is something special. I want to fight for California,” Luckey said during an invite-only press conference on Monday.
He added that he’s felt pressure from other billionaires to declare his intention to leave.
“This has been a point of friction between me and some of my other billionaire friends,” he said. “They’ve said things like ‘Palmer, you have to have solidarity for us. You can’t enable these really bad policies. If you stay and if you don’t leave, it’s going to show them that there’s no consequences.’ I empathize with that argument, but it’s not one that I’m going to participate in right now because I still believe that we can fix things.”
Luckey added that it’s not the idea of paying taxes that he takes issue with, but that the bill is sponsored by a specific union, a unit of the United Healthcare Workers, that wants to use the money the tax would raise “for their uses,” he said. The measure’s sponsors say the money will be used for “health care, education, and food assistance” programs in the state, and they specifically name Medi-Cal, California’s health coverage program for low-income residents.
Another issue for Luckey, as for others, is how the proposal would assess the tax owed, as well as the penalties. It would tax “wealth” including unrealized assets that haven’t been sold, and illiquid assets that are hard to turn into cash. And penalties can be assessed as high as 40%.
“It’s almost like a seizure of future wealth in that way. That’s not even the real problem. The biggest problem is the tax on control of your own company,” he said. According to the Tax Foundation, a tax policy think tank, the proposal would treat someone with voting control as owning at least that same share of the company. This would affect founders with super-voting shares, which carry extra votes per share, because they may own only a minority of the company. A founder with 40% of the votes but 10% of the ownership, for example, could be taxed as if they owned at least 40%, and selling all their shares might not cover the bill. (The measure’s drafters say that reading is mistaken, arguing that super-voting shares are publicly traded assets and are valued differently.)
“I’m a founder who’s raised a bunch of money, I’ve diluted myself a lot. I’ve given equity to my employees,” Luckey said of his own situation. “My employees have more equity in Anduril than me. I’ve given a lot of equity out to people, but what I have done is I’ve preserved the voting rights so that as those employees sell their shares to pay off their home loans or whatever, that the voting control doesn’t go to other people outside the company.”
He also said that if he were ever to leave, “I lose all those voting rights. My voting rights only stick as long as I’m an American citizen living in America, running Anduril.” The condition makes sense given that Anduril is primarily a defense contractor selling equipment to the U.S. military.
In Luckey’s case, he believes he could owe 5% of Anduril’s $61 billion, a bill of around $3 billion, just on that asset alone. (For comparison, Larry Page, the Google co-founder who did leave California, still has 27% voting control of Alphabet, Google’s parent company, which has a market value of just under $4 trillion.)
“But I’m planning on staying in California. I’m going to keep fighting it,” he said. “I’m hoping that this doesn’t pass. I’m hoping if it does pass, that there are legal challenges to say, ‘Hey, you can’t post facto seize people’s past and future wealth, nor can you tax their voting interests in their own company.’ That’s truly unprecedented. That is not a tax on ownership. It is a tax on control.”

articles.title: Anduril, Qualcomm launch BlueChip, a new kind of US-made laptop | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anduril founder Palmer Luckey is vowing to bring computer manufacturing back to the U.S. And by that, he doesn’t just mean assembly, but the production of every individual component, some of which are exclusively made in China today.
Anduril is partnering with Qualcomm to achieve that mission with a new computer called BlueChip, the companies announced Tuesday. BlueChip will be available for preorder in 2027.
While technical details are scant — Anduril hasn’t even finished contracting with all its component suppliers yet, according to Luckey — this first product will be a hardened laptop. It will be designed to withstand the most grueling physical environments and meet the security-conscious needs of the military, government, first responders, and law enforcement.
For the first generation, about 90% of its components will be made in the U.S. or in allied countries, Anduril says, most notably its CPU. BlueChip will run on a Snapdragon X Series built at TSMC’s massive new facility in Arizona. The CPU uses the same architecture that powers other laptops, including the Microsoft Surface, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon said during the press conference.
“As of right now, the laptop’s bill of materials is about 90% U.S. and allied [ally countries], and we have a technical roadmap to get to 100% domestic over time,” Luckey said. “The intent in the long run is to have an option that is made entirely in the United States, 100% domestic. And I mean everything. I mean the displays. I mean the metallics. I mean the the magnetics. All of it.”
Right now, for instance, Luckey says he’s found an American supplier for the glass that covers the display, but the display itself is one of several components he says are only manufactured in China.
While Luckey says consumers are welcome to order a BlueChip — the company may even create a waiting list for interested consumers — this first PC won’t be designed for them. For one thing, as a hardened computer, it will be heavy and have battery-life constraints because of the engineering required to withstand rain, dust, and other rugged conditions.
The bigger point is to offer U.S. government agencies a product that complies with regulations requiring them to buy U.S.-made computers. In this case, the selling point is a transparent supply chain that customers can track and audit.
“These computers are the anti-surveillance computer. You fully control it,” Luckey described in a recent interview. “You know everything that is in it, every single component, and you know every software component that is running on it.”
Anduril is also working to ensure that the Arm-based machine works well with Windows apps, apps built for certain Linux distributions used by the government, and even archaic software that various agencies still run.
While Anduril hasn’t yet announced pricing, Luckey estimates it will cost about 20% more than typical high-end PCs.
“As much as I love BlueChip, if I was just a normal consumer making a rational decision without a kind of patriotic basis, I’d be better off buying a Dell laptop than an Anduril laptop because it’s going to be cheaper. I’m just talking about your average-person consumer, right, who doesn’t have any real need for this,” Luckey said.
But Luckey clearly hopes Anduril will eventually make U.S.-made laptops more in line with consumer desires. He said the product is the first in what he envisions as a full line of BlueChip computers, noting that he began his career making virtual reality headsets for consumers.
“I’m buying American cars, and then I buy a computer that’s made on the other side of the world, not just China, but you know, Japan, Korea,” he said. “It’s kind of humiliating that as an American and my birthright is computers, in my opinion, because America invented them, that I’m not able to buy an American computer.”
As for the potentially expensive folly of trying to take on China’s electronics components manufacturing industry single-handedly, Luckey joked about his internal reputation for “being a nut” with such big ideas. (He admits that he pushed his board to spend $900 million to build a factory for a jet before the company had even won a contract.)
“This is not one of those things. My investors do not think I’m a crazy person in this particular area,” he said. In fact, rugged computers are already about a $5 billion market.

articles.title: Firefox’s Smart Window adds AI form filling and webpage monitoring
articles.text:
Mozilla is updating Smart Window — Firefox’s AI-powered browsing experience — with a new feature that can help you fill out online forms based on your open tabs. As an example, Mozilla says Smart Window can pull information from your online portfolio or LinkedIn page to paste your work history into a job application.
Firefox’s Smart Window adds AI form filling and webpage monitoring
An update to Firefox’s AI browsing experience can draw from your open tabs to help you fill out forms.
You can try out this feature by clicking into a form with at least four text fields. From there, you’ll see an option to “Fill from sources,” which will show all of the tabs Firefox will draw from. You can then select or deselect tabs that you want Firefox to use, and the browser will generate suggestions based on the information in them. This feature currently supports text fields on web forms, but Mozilla is working to add support for dropdown menus and PDFs. Mozilla notes that data from your source pages is shared with Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model that generates the text suggestions.
Along with this update, you can now ask Firefox’s Smart Window to watch a certain webpage for sales, new job listings, and other updates. You can set up a task by typing “/watch” in the Smart Window chat, describing what you’re looking for, and adding the webpages you want to watch. Firefox can then check for updates on a daily or weekly basis, but only when the browser is open.
When Firefox detects the change you’re looking for, it will send you a notification through the Tasks button on the toolbar, or on your desktop (if you have desktop notifications enabled). Firefox will pause watching for updates if it doesn’t detect a change after 60 days, before stopping them completely after 90 days.
These two features are rolling out to the Smart Window beta on desktop in the US and Canada. They’ll be available in other countries in the “coming months.”

articles.title: Major League Baseball is looking for a new kind of fan
articles.text:
On October 2nd, just as Major League Baseball’s Division Series was kicking off, the main MLB Instagram and TikTok accounts posted a video hyping up the teams still in the running for the World Series. It featured clips of players from the Milwaukee Brewers, Los Angeles Dodgers, Chicago White Sox, and more sliding into home plate, hitting homers, and celebrating hits — standard fare for a highlight reel. What really makes the montage, though, is that it’s set to an Olivia Rodrigo song.
Major League Baseball is looking for a new kind of fan
A sport historically averse to internet culture is finding success embracing fandom, trends, and influencers.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The song, “My Way,” is an album track — not even a single — from Rodrigo’s latest record. It’s not exactly the soundtrack one might expect from an MLB-produced video. (“And here is the part where the girl gets pissed / And the girl is me, did you get that hint?” she sings.) But as evidenced by the comments, it hit exactly the right people: “I see I’m part of a very niche part of MLB fans,” one person said. “Target audience reached,” another responded. The clip has over 2.1 million views on Instagram and 615,000 views on TikTok.
“One of our favorite things is when a community says, ‘Oh, MLB knows ball,’ or, ‘Oh, I can’t believe my interests [are] converging,’” says Cameron Gidari, MLB’s vice president of social media and innovation. The social team is a fan of Rodrigo’s to begin with and loves the song, Gidari says, “but then also we thought we could make a really interesting edit with it, and we thought that community would appreciate being seen.”
Acknowledging the combination of baseball–Olivia Rodrigo fans is smart. It also might be essential for the survival of the sport. People love baseball, of course, but it often feels like it’s trailing other sports, not just in viewership but also culturally. Baseball is famously stats heavy — there are thousands of games every season across the league, and teams play almost every day. What happens on the field today is often contextualized through what happened in games in the past, making it hard to jump in without a history of watching (or learning about) the sport. Go back a few years, and you’d find MLB social channels were more “editorially focused,” Gidari says, focusing on facts of the game or highlights. Speaking to fans who have other interests — or who are simply more casual — has been a deliberate choice, he says.
“Our tone overall on social is the tone of fandom,” Gidari says. “We think there is something really inviting and magnetic about that, and it was a conscious shift.”
Here’s a post of Dua Lipa and Callum Turner at a Yankees game, the night the team was eliminated from the postseason. Here’s an edit spliced together with shots of athletes looking shocked and in awe, as if they were reacting to a song by the K-pop group Stray Kids. Here’s a highlight reel of White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami being funny.
The nature of social media algorithms all but requires MLB to branch out. Recommendation-based social feeds mean that following an account doesn’t necessarily mean followers will see the content — feeds have become reorganized into content niches, topics, and trends, and Gidari says “really aggressive algorithm changes” meant the league had to rethink what it posts. Content from the MLB in English- and Spanish-language social accounts racked up 19.1 billion views during the 2026 regular season, Gidari says, a record.
A significant part of that shift has been MLB’s embrace of influencers and content creators. So far this year, the league has tapped 400 creators who posted a combined 3,800 pieces of content, and in the postseason, MLB has had content creators at every single game. The league expects to have 100 content creators at the World Series, depending on how many games it runs.
The openness and collaboration with content creators is relatively new for MLB. As recently as 2024, content creators (including Jimmy “Jomboy” O’Brien, who does viral lip-reading breakdowns) complained of getting wide-ranging copyright takedowns on their content. In 2025, Commissioner Rob Manfred acknowledged the league fumbled this slice of the fanbase and that changing its tune had been “a really good thing” for MLB. (The league even acquired a stake in O’Brien’s media company last year.) More recently, a TikTok partnership gave select creators access to the league’s archives to use in their content.
For the first time, MLB has expanded beyond having influencers only at big events. The league now brings content creators to regular season games, too, and has broadened its reach to include more than just baseball and sports creators. Rachel Richter, director of influencer strategy, says MLB works with food, fashion, lifestyle, gaming, and family influencers, too.
“There are casual fans or [people] that aren’t even fans yet, that maybe they’re going to go to a game just because they get to put on a cute outfit, or they want to try this new food item,” Richter says. The idea is to get those creators to a game and let them incorporate baseball into their usual content.
The league is building on momentum, especially coming off a successful season last year: Game 7 of the 2025 World Series between the Dodgers and the Toronto Blue Jays was the most-watched World Series game since 2017, and more international viewers watched last year’s matchup than ever before. But as other sports have found, it can be a learning curve to balance longtime fans and the culture of the sport with an insurgent, at times unpredictable, class of promotional power brokers: The biggest story out of this year’s US Open, for example, was not the tennis itself but the many complaints and debates about the influencers who attended.
MLB is working to expand what constitutes a fan, reaching into corners of the internet and culture that previously were ignored or, at the very least, untapped. At the same time, it’s hurtling toward an uncertain 2027 season as the collective bargaining agreement between team owners and the MLB Players Association is set to expire in December. If the union and owners don’t reach a deal in time, players likely would be locked out, and the 2027 season could be shortened. Messaging that conflict would be a challenge in itself for the league — especially after adopting the voice of new, casual, and eager fans who are looking for a reason to tune in.
Correction, October 27th: Corrected a misspelling of Gidari’s name.

articles.title: Apple puts its M6 chip in a new iMac and entry-level MacBook Pro
articles.text:
Apple’s latest iMac looks much like the previous one, but the company has packed a new M6 chip into its 24-inch all-in-one desktop, promising faster graphics, more processing power and a substantial boost in on-device AI performance.
The new iMac is available to pre-order from Wednesday in 35 countries, with deliveries and in-store availability starting on November 6.
The familiar design remains intact, including the thin body and seven colour options: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver. Most of the changes are under the hood.
The M6 chip comes with up to 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores, two more of each than the M4 in the previous model. Apple claims it delivers the fastest single-core CPU performance of any computer, based on its own tests.
The bigger change is how the chip handles AI. Each GPU core now includes a Neural Accelerator designed to speed up AI workloads, working alongside a 16-core Neural Engine.
Apple says this combination makes on-device AI tasks up to five times faster than on the M4 iMac. Graphics performance in photo editing is up to twice as fast.
Apple’s other performance claims include spreadsheets in Microsoft Excel running up to 1.5 times faster, ray-traced games running up to twice as fast, and storage reading and writing data at up to twice the previous speed.
The company is also targeting people still using older desktops. It says the M6 iMac is up to 18 times faster than the most popular Intel-based iMac.
Compared with the M1 model released in 2021, Apple claims up to 2.5 times the performance in Excel and up to 12 times the on-device AI performance.
The 24-inch 4.5K display is unchanged, with a maximum brightness of 500 nits. Buyers choosing the 12-core configuration can opt for nano-texture glass, which reduces glare.
Connectivity gets a more substantial update as the new iMac supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, while the 12-core version adds 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet and four Thunderbolt 4 ports. It can also drive two external 6K displays.
Moreover, the company has kept the 12-megapixel Center Stage camera, six-speaker sound system and three-microphone array. A matching keyboard and either a mouse or trackpad are included, with the 12-core model getting a keyboard with Touch ID.
“iMac raises the bar yet again,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of hardware engineering.
The desktop ships with macOS 27, which introduces Apple’s new AI-powered Siri to the Mac. The assistant can answer questions, search through messages, emails and photos, and perform actions across apps.
Siri AI remains in beta, supports six languages, and comes with daily usage limits. Apple plans to offer additional access for a fee later. The assistant first arrived on the iPhone with iOS 27.2. macOS 27 also includes writing tools and a way to organise Safari tabs by topic.
Those prices match what the M4 iMac cost immediately before launch, but they are higher than the original prices for that model.
Apple raised iMac prices by $200 in June as memory and storage costs climbed amid demand from AI data centres, according to EveryMac. Before that increase, the cheapest model cost $1,299.
Apple also said the new iMac’s stand uses 100% recycled aluminium, while its magnets use 100% recycled rare earth elements.
The iMac was not the only Mac to get an update: Apple also unveiled an M6 MacBook Pro. Meanwhile, its new foldable phone has attracted complaints about cracked screens.

articles.title: Indian investors rush to Nvidia, SpaceX, Apple as local trading apps roll out access to U.S. stocks
articles.text:
Major Indian online investment platforms are unlocking access to U.S. stocks for millions of retail investors eager to diversify into global assets as the country's markets continue to underperform.
Earlier, access to U.S. markets and exchange-traded funds was limited to wealthier Indians, via global banks and wealth management firms.
Groww, an Indian investment platform that accounts for more than 29% of the country's 46 million active investors across stock brokerages, rolled out the U.S. equity trading feature earlier this month, Harsh Jain, chief operating officer and co-founder of the company, told CNBC.
NVIDIA, SpaceX, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Micron and Meta are the most popular companies among early users, Jain said, whose firm has provided access to more than 10,000 U.S. stocks, exchange-traded funds and fractional share ownership.
Zerodha, the second-largest trading platform with a 15% share of active clients as per NSE data, has also started beta testing access to U.S. stocks and plans to launch in a few weeks, the company told CNBC.
Another popular brokerage with 6.7 million active retail clients, Angel One, is also reportedly planning to launch U.S. stock trading on its platform.
There is a "big interest" among Indians to invest in U.S. stocks, especially in tech companies, Nitin Jain, chief executive and director at Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Singapore, told CNBC. He added that "retail investors like whatever goes up," pointing to the frenzy among Indian investors for investing in crypto a few years back.
U.S. stocks in demand
"There has always been latent demand in India for investing in global companies," Somnath Mukherjee, vice president of corporate development at Zerodha, told CNBC.
He said that the underperformance of the Indian stock market over the past few years and the lack of local artificial intelligence champions is driving the demand for U.S offerings. The depreciation of the Indian rupee against the dollar is also pushing investors "to keep a part of their portfolio in another currency," Mukherjee said.
India's benchmark stock index, the Nifty 50, has dropped nearly 13% since the start of the year while the S&P 500 has gained over 12%. Foreign investors are fleeing the country's markets, with a record $32.5 billion in outflows in direct equities since January, as per data from Indian depository NSDL, pressuring the stock market.
With the absence of any major AI company and relatively expensive valuations, investors have picked markets such as South Korea and Taiwan over India, experts said.
In August, resident Indians sent over $321 million overseas for investing in equity and debt, up 111% from a year ago, according to the Indian central bank's data. In the financial year ended March 2026, outward remittances for investments in equity and debt stood at $2.6 billion.
While the retail outflows are a small fraction of India's currency reserves, the worry is that they rise exactly when the rupee is weak, and US markets look strong, and thereby "amplify pressure at the worst moment," Tanvi Kanchan, associate director, head of international business and strategy, Anand Rathi Shares & Stock Brokers said.
Investment now accounts for about 11.7% of total outward remittances, up from 5.8% a year ago, so Indians are shifting from spending abroad to investing abroad, Kanchan said.
The exit of foreign investors and rising energy bills due to the Iran war have already hit the Indian currency, warranting the central bank to step in. Kotak's Jain cautioned that as participation increases, the Indian regulator could have "second thoughts" around allowing retail access to U.S. markets.

articles.title: SK Hynix third-quarter profit sharply beats estimates on AI memory boost
articles.text:
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix on Wednesday released its third-quarter earnings results, posting a record high quarterly profit that sharply beats estimates, while announcing over $25 billion in dividends and buybacks.
Here are SK Hynix's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:
- Revenue: 104.62 trillion won ($78.86 billion) vs. 98.34 trillion won expected
- Operating profit: 83.33 trillion won vs. 76.72 trillion won expected
Revenue rose 327.9% from a year earlier, while operating profit climbed 632.1% year on year.
Compared with the previous quarter, revenue climbed 31.9%, while operating profit surged 37.6%.
SK Hynix posted record quarterly revenue and operating profit, with sales exceeding 100 trillion won for the first time, as it announced plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders — including at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won in share buybacks and cancellations.
The chipmaker approved a third-quarter dividend of 14 trillion won, including a special dividend funded by gains from its investment in Kioxia. The company will also buyback 20 trillion won in shares, half of which will be cancelled this year.
SK Hynix expects HBM4 to surpass HBM3E in both shipments and revenue in the fourth quarter, as it ramps up production at its M15X facility in Cheongju, South Korea.
HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is a type of advanced memory used alongside AI processors to handle large amounts of data. HBM4 is the sixth generation of the technology.
The company has secured long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than 50% of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028.
It expects memory demand to outpace supply through 2030 and plans to significantly increase investment next year.
In August, SK Hynix had announced plans to repurchase and cancel 40 trillion won worth of its own shares, while raising its shareholder return target to more than 50% of cumulative free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027.
Last week, SK Hynix announced that its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm would halt its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and IPO options, citing market volatility and share price trends.
The company said it would continue to assess investment timing, scale and financing options to support Solidigm's growth and enhance shareholder value.

articles.title: Where Cramer stands on two beaten-down aerospace stocks — and the one to buy
articles.text:
The recent sell-off in aerospace stocks could be creating opportunities for investors willing to look beyond the industry's near-term challenges, CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday.
The group has been under pressure for months as higher oil prices and interest rates raise concerns about demand for new aircraft. Rising fuel costs squeeze airline profits — potentially forcing carriers to cut routes and scale back aircraft purchases. Higher rates make financing new planes more expensive, adding to those demand worries.
Even with gains of more than 3% on Tuesday, GE Aerospace is down 23% from its 52-week high of nearly $389 per share on Aug. 6. The stock is down 3% year to date. Boeing's slide of more than 10% on Tuesday put the CNBC Investing Club stock down 23% in 2026. For comparison, the iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (ITA) is down roughly 4% year to date, while the broader market S&P 500 is up over 12.5% in 2026.
"If you're willing to look long-term here, I still think this sector will be a secular, long-term winner," the "Mad Money" host said. "The idea that higher fuel prices and higher interest rates will kill demand just looks flat-out wrong." Here's a closer look at where Cramer stands on the stocks.
GE Aerospace delivered a strong third quarter last week but still couldn't catch a break. Cramer sees the weakness as a buying opportunity, pointing to robust demand for the company's jet engines. Orders in GE's commercial aerospace business surged 58%, including a 235% increase in equipment orders, pushing its backlog to $170 billion.
"Remember, the big concern for the Aerospace sector – the reason these stocks have been falling for the past couple of months – is the idea that higher oil prices and interest rates will result in fewer plane orders and, thus, fewer jet engine orders for GE," Cramer said. "But those incredible order numbers from GE – especially on the Commercial side, and for new equipment – show it's clearly not the case."
The quarter wasn't without its shortcomings. Free cash flow fell 14% year over year and came in slightly below expectations, while GE's valuation remains elevated at roughly 37 times the midpoint of its updated full-year earnings guidance.
"When you have a lofty multiple like this, it has to be a clean 'beat-and-raise' and we didn't get that," Cramer said. Still, he said the strength of GE's underlying business outweighs those concerns. "GE looks fine to buy now."
Cramer was more cautious on Boeing.
While reporting a generally mixed third quarter on Tuesday, free cash flow did beat estimates. FCF is the metric to watch in Boeing turnaround efforts. However, it was remarks on the earnings call that sent the stock to 52-week lows. Management outlined a multiyear outlook on free cash flow that fell short of expectations, partly because of upfront spending tied to a new contract to develop next-generation fighter jets for the U.S. Navy. Executives also said the company would not significantly ramp up 737 Max production until late next year.
"I'm hopeful that this reset can be a clearing event," Cramer said. "Some investors will give up, but everyone who remains will be using a new, more realistic set of free cash flow targets going forward."
Still, Cramer pointed to Boeing's substantial order backlog as evidence that demand for aircraft remains strong. The company received 300 net commercial aircraft orders during the quarter, bringing its commercial backlog to more than 6,300 planes valued at a record $612 billion. The company's defense backlog also reached a record $101 billion.
While facing a tougher road ahead than GE Aerospace and its shares could slip further, Cramer does remain optimistic about Boeing's longer-term prospects, provided management can deliver on its revised targets.

articles.title: Jim Cramer warns investors not to get fooled by the latest AI stock rally
articles.text:
CNBC's Jim Cramer warned Tuesday that investors may be getting ahead of themselves by declaring the artificial intelligence trade back on track.
AI-related stocks rallied for a second straight session, fueled by renewed enthusiasm for chipmakers after a group of banks and Blackstone announced $63 billion in financing for Anthropic to purchase Broadcom's computing hardware. The gains followed Monday's rally, sparked in part by Anthropic's S-1 filing. But Cramer cautioned the renewed optimism doesn't resolve the pressures facing the data center trade, which was hit hard late last week.
"I'm pleased that people feel so comfortable that tech is all good to go because there is money flowing back in," the "Mad Money" host said. "I don't think that's a reason to call all clear. I think it's a reason to look at other sectors in the economy."
Cramer's skepticism centers on three lingering risks.
First, Cramer remains concerned about smaller AI infrastructure companies, known as neoclouds, that are taking on significant debt to fund the data center build-out. Rising interest rates have intensified worries about their ability to sustain those borrowing costs. Cramer singled out CoreWeave, whose bonds have yielded as much as 15%, along with Nebius and Iren. Despite an almost 8% rebound in CoreWeave shares Tuesday, he warned that fresh negativity around CoreWeave could emerge.
"I have learned that after every positive story about anything in the data center, there will be a plethora of negative stories about something wrong, including Coreweave," Cramer said.
Second, Cramer questioned whether the Broadcom-Anthropic financing deal was as reassuring as investors believed. While the $63 billion package demonstrated that lenders were still willing to finance massive AI investments, Cramer raised concerns that Anthropic is borrowing money to buy Broadcom's technology, rather than paying for it with profits from its own business. "People don't seem to grasp that [Anthropic] got the money in the Broadcom-arranged financing deal to purchase equipment from Broadcom," he said.
Finally, Cramer said that Tuesday's calmer bond market could prove short-lived. Oil prices declined and the 10-year Treasury yield fell below 5%, easing some pressure on AI companies that need to borrow heavily to fund their data center investments. But those conditions could reverse, particularly with the Federal Reserve set to announce its latest interest rate decision Wednesday afternoon, followed by Chairman Kevin Warsh's post-meeting press conference. The midterm elections next week and potential flare-ups in the Middle East may represent additional sources of volatility.
"With the exception of Nvidia, these data center companies don't have a lot of money. So they have to borrow the money," Cramer said. "The rates are getting so high that the return is getting uncertain. That hasn't changed at all."
Cramer emphasized that he remains "an unabashed believer in the AI build-out." But until the industry's financing challenges ease, he isn't ready to declare the coast clear.
